title: Preparing pre-service teachers to understand and address cybersecurity challenges and promote digital citizenship in resource-constrained educational contexts: the role of 21st-century skills and technological knowledge
abstract: The availability and use of affordable mobile technologies offer significant opportunities for teachers to integrate technologies in their teaching, particularly in resource-constrained contexts. However, the availability and affordability of these digital tools do not guarantee their effective use. Their use also exposes teachers and learners to cybersecurity risks, and how well pre-service teachers (PSTs) are prepared to deal with those risks cannot be assumed. This study examines how PSTs are prepared to understand and address cybersecurity challenges and to promote digital citizenship in resource-constrained educational contexts. Preparation is examined along two dimensions: the 21st-century skills that PSTs demonstrate and the technological knowledge (TK) they acquire. This study was guided by the Cybersecurity Curriculum Framework, which integrates Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK), Digital Citizenship, and 21st-century skills. A qualitative approach was used. title: Empowering future educators: integrating artificial intelligence, sustainability, and ethics into teacher preparation programs
abstract: Teacher preparation programs have quickly adopted artificial intelligence tools, but the ethical, social, and environmental dimensions of that adoption receive comparatively little attention in how future educators are trained. This conceptual analysis addresses that gap by asking how AI competence, sustainability education, and ethical technology use can be integrated into teacher preparation as a single coherent framework rather than three parallel add-ons. Drawing on critical digital pedagogy, domain-specific cognition theory, and Mezirow's transformative learning theory, we synthesize policy documents and peer-reviewed literature on AI in education, sustainability education, and teacher preparation to develop the SAGE Model (Sustainability and AI for Global Educators). title: From eugenics to algorithms: structural racism in STEM and the imperative of liberatory reconstruction
abstract: This article argues that the exclusion of Black and other racially minoritized people from STEM is neither accidental nor remedied through incremental diversification. STEM's foundational structures includes its eugenics-entangled statistical canon, color-blind policy regimes, and systematic misdiagnosis of structural harm as individual deficit form an interlocking design of racial subordination. A primary argument for this article is that diversification without structural transformation is packaged and delivered as false prophets. Drawing on scholarship in critical race theory, Afrofuturism, critical quantitative and computational methodologies, and the mental and physical outcomes of these racialized STEM experiences, this article traces the historical construction of scientific racism from eugenics through contemporary algorithmic systems that perpetuate racial hierarchy under the sign of objectivity. title: Developing interdisciplinary and meta-subject competencies in school geography: a systematic review of digital and mobile learning approaches
abstract: The integration of digital and mobile learning approaches into school geography has become an important direction of pedagogical innovation in recent years, however, how these approaches systematically develop interdisciplinary and meta-subject competencies remains insufficiently theorized and empirically developed. Although individual studies have demonstrated the pedagogical potential of geospatial technologies, mobile augmented reality, immersive virtual environments, and artificial intelligence-based platforms, no previous review has conducted a comprehensive, systematic analysis of this body of evidence, linking it to the cross-curricular and meta-subject competency frameworks that are central to the reform agenda for national and international curricula. title: Automated and AI-assisted assessment and perceived fairness in a polyethnic university: digitalization as a potential pathway to interethnic equity in Kazakhstan's higher education
abstract: The digital transformation of higher education in Kazakhstan unfolds against the backdrop of the 2022 constitutional reforms and the policy agenda of building a “Just Kazakhstan,” in which equal access to education for a multiethnic student population is a declared priority. This study examines how university students evaluate the fairness of automated and AI-assisted assessment, and whether such technologies are seen as reducing subjectivity, corruption risks, and ascriptive (ethnic and linguistic) bias. Respondents were not asked to compare formats within a single item, so the study reports perceptions of automated assessment rather than a measured contrast with examiner-based assessment. A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 300 undergraduate and graduate students at a large public pedagogical university in Almaty (June 2026). title: Educator and AI agent communication in AI-mediated higher education classrooms: a mini review along the complementarity-substitution axis
abstract: The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence into higher education classrooms has reignited the debate over the role of communication between educators and students. This mini-review synthesizes the role of instructional communication constructs (immediacy, rapport, clarity, and credibility) and the relational functions they deliver in AI-mediated classrooms, based on 32 peer-reviewed studies published after 2023, identified through a large-scale literature search (using Scopus and Web of Science-based indexes, OpenAlex, and ERIC). The findings fall into three main categories. First, educator communication behaviors continue to predict student outcomes; a recent meta-analysis reports a moderate-to-large association (r = 0.443), although the evidence base is concentrated in Chinese and EFL samples. Second, students evaluate AI agents using human communication categories, but a systematic gap emerges in the dimension of goodwill, which is partially bridged by cues of immediacy and politeness. title: Artificial intelligence as a constructivist scaffold in anaesthesia education: a mini review
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), including generative AI and large language models, is increasingly used in health professions education, but evidence for educational benefit in anaesthesia remains limited and heterogeneous. This focused Mini Review incorporates literature identified through August 2026 and distinguishes anaesthesia-specific empirical evidence from feasibility studies, extrapolation from broader health professions education, and proposed applications. Using constructivist learning theory, we conceptualise AI not as an autonomous teacher or objective assessor, but as a contingent and temporary scaffold that should be adapted to learner performance, progressively faded, and followed by assessment of independent transfer. We further integrate cognitive apprenticeship through modelling, coaching, articulation, reflection, and exploration while maintaining the essential role of human supervisors. title: Online learning self-efficacy and self-regulated learning in relation to perceived cognitive and academic performance in digital learning: an explanatory sequential mixed-methods study at five Vietnamese universities
abstract: Introduction This explanatory sequential mixed-methods study examined associations of self-regulated learning (SRL) and online learning self-efficacy with perceived academic and cognitive performance among undergraduates recruited from five Vietnamese universities. Methods The quantitative phase analyzed 685 complete survey responses obtained through quota-guided convenience sampling and tested a four-construct covariance-based structural equation model. The qualitative phase involved 24 interview participants purposively selected from the survey pool to contextualize the observed structural associations. Results The measurement model showed good fit on the retained indices (χ²/df = 2.15, CFI = .962, TLI = .958, RMSEA = .041, SRMR = .038). SRL was positively associated with perceived academic performance ( β = .51) and perceived cognitive performance (β = .44), while online learning self-efficacy was associated with perceived academic performance ( β = .24) and perceived cognitive performance ( β = .36), all p < .001. title: Asynchronish: blending synchronous and asynchronous strategies for engaging online mathematics education students
abstract: This article explores the innovative “asynchronish” approach to online mathematics and teacher education, blending synchronous and asynchronous elements to enhance student engagement and sense of belonging. Drawing from experiences in mathematics and teacher education courses, we examine two key engagement strategies: (1) utilizing collaborative platforms like Slack and (2) creating opportunities for online small-group discussions. Grounded in Garrison's Community of Inquiry framework, this study examines evidence-based strategies for fostering interactive virtual learning environments that enhance cognitive and social connectivity in online mathematics and teacher education courses through analysis of implementation data and student responses.

title: Factors and predictors of educational inequalities in European schools: a systematic literature review with a longitudinal lens
abstract: Background Ensuring equal access to quality education is essential for building fair and inclusive societies. However, educational inequalities persist across and within European countries, despite numerous policy initiatives aimed at addressing them. Objectives This systematic review aims to identify and categorise variables of educational inequalities in European primary and secondary schools, focusing on studies with longitudinal or repeated cross-sectional designs. Methods Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, 1,399 studies published from 1995 to 2024 in seven European languages were identified through Scopus, Google Scholar, repositories of international organisations and citation mining. After a two-step screening, 157 studies that met the predefined criteria were analysed in depth using a review matrix. Inter-rater reliability checks ensured consistency. Results Despite targeted policy measures to enhance fairness and inclusion, inequalities remain widespread across European schools. title: Sustainable digitalization in education: perspectives of Latvian educational professionals
abstract: Introduction The fields of education and sustainable development are currently facing several challenges resulting from the rapid development of digital technologies. Education is considered a fundamental prerequisite both for achieving sustainable development and for fostering the meaningful and responsible use of digital technologies. However, the role of digital technologies in promoting sustainable development has often been approached in a narrow and superficial manner. This study explores perceptions of digital sustainability (“digitainability”) among Latvian educational professionals. Methods The research involved semi-structured interviews with Latvian teachers ( n = 3) and a focus group discussion with school representatives ( n = 5). The qualitative data were analyzed using thematic analysis. Results The findings indicate that professionals' views on the role of digital technologies in promoting sustainability are predominantly focused on individual projects and isolated activities rather than on a systematic and long-term strategic approach. title: Empowering student-led climate solutions: the role of AI in STEAM education
abstract: This convergent mixed-methods study investigates the strategic integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into a university-level STEAM curriculum to empower students to design climate solutions. Combining quantitative survey data from 69 undergraduate students selected via a complete cohort census sampling approach (response rate: 84.1%) and multi-tiered purposive qualitative interviews with N = 25 participants ( N = 11 experts, N = 9 faculty members, and N = 5 student innovators), the findings indicate high technological familiarity and widespread adoption (100% AI tool use). Specifically, students reported the highest agreement for AI enhancing their creativity and learning independence (86.9%, M = 4.12), supporting their capacity to pivot from data collection to strategic solution design (73.9%, M = 3.78), and bolstering their perceived empowerment to propose climate solutions (76.8%, M = 3.84). title: Institutional governance and perceived curriculum quality in Somaliland higher education: an exploratory cross-sectional analysis
abstract: Background Somaliland's university system has moved from community-led post-conflict reconstruction toward national regulation and quality assurance, yet evidence on curriculum governance remains limited. Purpose This exploratory study examined associations between archived composite scores for Institutional Curriculum Governance and Support (ICGS) and perceived Curriculum Development Quality and Effectiveness (CDQE) among respondents from six universities. Methods The archived analytic dataset comprised 358 respondents (245 students and 113 academic staff). Descriptive statistics and ordinary least squares regressions were used; HC3 standard errors were applied to the pooled and academic-staff construct models where heteroscedasticity had been detected. The complete English dissertation questionnaire and its five-point response scales were recovered, but the item-to-construct codebook, scoring rules, validation records, and respondent-level file needed for independent measurement and clustering analyses were unavailable. title: A qualitative inquiry on redefining students' assessments in the age of artificial intelligence: academicians' viewpoint
abstract: Purpose Artificial Intelligence (AI) presents new opportunities and challenges, and its adoption has transformed learning and development for students. Current studies have mostly explored the use of AI among students, with very little emphasis on its impact on teaching and learning tasks, academicians' professional identities, and student-teacher interaction. This research examines the pedagogical, professional, and institutional implications of students' use of AI from the perspective of academic staff at private universities in Malaysia. Design A structured interview protocol with ten open-ended questions was adopted to implement the qualitative exploratory research design. The final sample consisted of 18 academicians with at least 5 years of teaching experience in higher education and who have been involved in assessing undergraduate, master's, and postgraduate students' assignments. Data were analyzed through open coding, axial coding, and thematic analysis. title: Self-regulated learning in the development of teachers' digital competencies—a systematic literature review
abstract: Introduction Digitalization places growing demands on teachers needing to prepare young people for life in increasingly digital environments. Challenges such as limited resources for teacher training and fast-paced developments in the field make self-regulated learning indispensable for equipping teachers with the necessary digital competences. Methods This study investigates the state of the art in this field and explores the interrelation of teachers' professional digital competence with self-regulated learning through a systematic literature review. Findings from the analysis of 17 studies published between 2009 and 2023 were analyzed. Results The reviewed works indicate a strong relationship between the concepts of digital competence and self-regulated learning through metacognition and highlight promising approaches for supporting preservice and in-service teachers in developing their digital competences in a self-regulated manner. title: The AI–UDL nexus in teacher education: designing inclusive learning for student variability
abstract: Introduction The modern higher education classroom is incredibly diverse, with students displaying various strengths, challenges, prior knowledge, and learning preferences. Traditional “one-size-fits-all” teaching methods often fail to meet different learners' needs and hinder student engagement and academic achievement. To address this, Universal Design for Learning (UDL), a research-based, learner-focused approach grounded in cognitive neuroscience, provides a proactive path to design more inclusive and accessible teaching practices. Methods Employing a quasi-experimental design, this study examined written lesson-planning performance among 45 Moroccan pre-service English as a Foreign Language (EFL) teachers across three conditions: a control group (CG), a UDL-only training group (TG1), and a UDL training supplemented with AI tools group (TG2). Results Analysis of the 38 participants with matched pretest and posttest scores indicated an adjusted between-group difference in posttest lesson-plan scores. title: Gamification and self-regulated learning in digital educational environments: a systematic review using an engagement dynamics–systems integration lens
abstract: This systematic review synthesises empirical evidence from 2020 onward on gamification for SRL in digital educational environments through an integrative analytical lens, Engagement Dynamics – Systems Integration (ED-SI). SRL is the single focal construct; self-directed learning and learner autonomy served only as search synonyms, and studies were retained only where the measured construct mapped onto self-regulatory processes. 44 empirical studies were identified using PRISMA 2020 guidelines by searching Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, IEEE Xplore, and ACM Digital Library from January 2020 to December 2025. Educational level was coded as an analytical dimension rather than used as an eligibility filter; the corpus spans primary through adult education, with higher education the largest stratum. Methodological quality was assessed with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT), and findings were synthesised narratively in line with Synthesis Without Meta-analysis (SWiM) guidance. title: The influence of music on affective, social, and motivational experiences during circuit training in physical education
abstract: Background/purpose The role of music in physical education (PE) is underexplored. This study investigated the effects of self-selected versus externally provided music on affect, emotions, social connectedness, and intrinsic motivation during PE lessons. Method A clustered cross-over design was used during circuit training in physical education, with a repeated-measures factor (music vs. no music) and a between-subjects factor (self-selected vs. provided music). Affective and social variables were assessed pre- and post-lesson; intrinsic motivation was measured post-lesson. The sample comprised 161 students ( M age = 10.85, SD age = 0.84). title: Psychological well-being and intrinsic motivation in initial teacher education: the influence of employment status, enrolment motives, and early teaching vocation
abstract: Introduction Psychological well-being and intrinsic motivation play an important role in academic engagement, professional identity development, and commitment to the teaching profession. However, limited evidence is available on how employment status, reasons for enrolment, and early vocational orientation are jointly associated with these constructs among students in initial teacher education. This study examined psychological well-being and intrinsic motivation among postgraduate students enrolled in Master's Degree programmes in Secondary Teacher Education. Methods A total of 239 postgraduate students enrolled at the University of Castilla-La Mancha and Villanueva University (Spain) participated in the study. Participants completed Ryff's Psychological Well-Being Scale and the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory (IMI). Independent-samples t-tests were conducted to examine differences in psychological well-being and intrinsic motivation according to employment status, reasons for enrolment, and early teaching vocation. title: Technology acceptance of artificial intelligence for cognitive assessment in autism spectrum disorder: a structural equation modeling approach with robustness and predictive analytics
abstract: Introduction Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition for which cognitive assessment can be time-consuming, resource intensive, and subject to interpretation. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers potential advantages in accuracy, efficiency, and usability, but human-centered factors influencing acceptance remain insufficiently examined. Methods This study examined healthcare and education professionals' perceptions of AI-based versus traditional cognitive assessment for ASD using a multi-method analytical framework. A final sample of 77 participants was analyzed after three outliers were removed. The analysis integrated PLS-SEM, fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA), PLSpredict, and robustness analyses to examine structural relationships, configurational pathways, predictive relevance, mediation, and moderation. Results AI-based assessment was perceived as more accurate, time-efficient, and user-friendly than traditional assessment. title: Quality in early childhood education and care: relationships with pedagogical dynamics profiles
abstract: Introduction Research has consistently highlighted key pedagogical dynamics that shape children's engagement, exploration, and learning. Crucial elements include the flow of daily routines, opportunities for child agency and participation, and the intentional integration of indoor and outdoor learning contexts. The aim of this study was to use a person-centered approach to identify profiles of pedagogical dynamics in Portuguese ECEC contexts and to examine how these profiles relate to professionals’ perceived quality of the organization of the educational environment. title: Developing and evaluating a creativity-oriented labor education course for students in Guangdong higher vocational colleges
abstract: Cultivating creativity through labor education in Guangdong higher vocational colleges is essential, yet existing courses often neglect higher-order creative thinking in favor of routine task completion. This study aimed to identify creativity-oriented competency indicators and develop, implement, and evaluate a novel labor education course integrating Tyler's curriculum model and Williams’ creativity framework. Utilizing a Research and Development (R&D) design with an exploratory sequential mixed-methods approach, the study progressed through four phases. Phase I involved a contextual study surveying 400 students and interviewing 12 instructors. Phase II focused on course development and pilot testing ( n = 25). Phase III implemented an intervention comparing an experimental group ( n = 15) to a comparison group ( n = 15). Phase IV evaluated post-course perceptions ( n = 25). Phase I identified key competency indicators, including technical and problem-solving skills, work ethics, social responsibility, and vocational skills. title: Playful and physically active mathematics learning in primary education: an exploratory comparison of pupils in schools with and without the darts math program
abstract: Introduction The aim of this study was to compare mathematical performance and cognitive abilities among third- and fourth-grade pupils attending schools with established use of the Darts Math Program (DMP) and pupils attending schools following the general mathematics program (GP). Methods This cross-sectional, non-randomized comparative study included 124 pupils from four primary schools in Northern Hungary (DMP: n = 70; GP: n = 54). Schools were purposively selected, and DMP exposure was determined by pre-existing school-level implementation. Curriculum-aligned mathematics assessments and selected tasks from the Gyarmathy Cognitive Profile Test were administered. title: Quality of systematic reviews on teaching English as a foreign language: a methodological review protocol
abstract: In many educational contexts worldwide, English is taught as a foreign (i.e., non-native, second, or additional) language. Teaching English as a foreign language, therefore, differs substantially from teaching English as a native language and relies on distinct approaches, methods, and strategies. Although systematic reviews are a key instrument for informing evidence-based educational practice and policy, evidence synthesis products in English language teaching are less accessible and show greater variability in methodological quality than those focused on teaching English as a native language. This study presents a protocol for a future methodological review aimed at assessing the methodological quality of systematic reviews on teaching English as a foreign language. The target population includes children, pupils, and students learning English as a foreign language within preschool through higher education. Only systematic reviews will be included; scoping reviews, integrative reviews, literature reviews, and all types of non-systematic reviews will be excluded. title: Early warning of academic risk from the first four weeks of online learning activity and assessment performance: a leakage-controlled, demographic-data-minimizing study on the OULAD benchmark
abstract: Early warning systems may identify academic risk while support remains possible, but published evaluations often use late-course data, sensitive background information, or leakage-prone splits. We tested prediction from the first four weeks of virtual learning environment activity and assessment performance, quantified the contribution of background/administrative data, and examined transfer across cohorts and modules. Using the Open University Learning Analytics Dataset (32,593 enrollments; analytic n = 27,553 still registered at day 28; 10.7 million activity records), we predicted failure or subsequent withdrawal from 13 behavioral and 9 background/administrative features. Splits and bootstrap resampling were grouped by student, with model selection by grouped cross-validation. The selected in-pool model reached ROC-AUC 0.7747 (student-cluster 95% CI 0.7624–0.7870); behavior alone reached 0.7504, a difference of 0.0243 (95% CI 0.0165–0.0321). title: A qualitative examination of the mediating void: teacher PCK, classroom management, and mathematical achievement
abstract: Recent quantitative literature in mathematics education has exposed a critical empirical paradox: neither classroom management nor mastery-oriented instructional practices statistically mediate the relationship between teachers' Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK) and secondary student achievement. Because quantitative designs rely on standardized numerical surveys, they frequently treat the interactive classroom environment as a black box, leaving the operational mechanisms behind this statistical breakdown completely unexplained. To address this literature gap, this interpretive qualitative multi-case study investigated the lived experiences of secondary school students within the Kumasi Metropolis of Ghana to explore why traditional structural optimization fails to translate into conceptual understanding. Four distinct public Senior High School mathematics classrooms characterized by highly qualified instructors yet uneven student performance were selected as bounded cases. Data collection was thoroughly triangulated over a two-month period using non-participant classroom observations, four student focus group discussions ( n = 32 ), and four semi-structured teacher interviews.

title: Who's in charge? The history and future of teacher learning orientation measures
abstract: Education grapples with two essential orientations to instruction: teacher-centered and student-centered; each has important strengths and weaknesses for children's learning. This narrative review concerns how these two learning orientations (LOs) have been measured in research by examining 75 years of Likert scale LO measures. Candidate instruments were identified through iterative database and reference-list searches, and were retained if they used a Likert scale format, applied to teaching generally rather than a specific subject, yielded scores for exactly two orientations, had undergone formal scale development, and had been used by researchers other than the scale's developer. Fifteen instruments met these criteria. We organize them into five dominant perspectives or theoretical frameworks: progressivism, teacher control and student autonomy, developmental, constructivism, and teacher/student-centered and -oriented. title: Supporting students beyond the classroom: faculty knowledge and practices in referring students to campus counseling services
abstract: Introduction College students face increasing mental health challenges, often placing faculty on the front lines of student support. However, instructors frequently feel unequipped to identify distress and refer students to campus counseling services. Method The present study ( N = 105) examined relationships among faculty demographics, referral training, referral history, location and services of the campus counseling center, mental health knowledge, and referral behaviors at an urban public university. Participants varied in faculty rank, academic department, years at college, and full- and part-time employment. Results Descriptive analyses indicated that referrals were made across all faculty regardless of gender, age, rank, department, longevity at the college, and employment status. Chi-square tests revealed no significant demographic, employment, or training predictors for making referrals. title: Reengineering organizational systems and culture for teacher learning: a co-design study in an urban school district
abstract: This qualitative study examines how a district-level secondary science education leader in a large urban United States school district engaged in co-design to reconsider organizational systems and conditions supporting teacher learning during the implementation of state-adopted science standards. Grounded in organizational sensemaking and co-design, the study conceptualizes leadership practice as the ongoing interpretation and redesign of system conditions that shape teaching and learning. In partnership with a team of researchers, the leader co-developed and implemented a survey as a diagnostic tool to capture teachers’ perspectives, challenges, and goals related to standards-aligned instruction. The co-design process provided contextual relevance while positioning the development of the diagnostic tool as a site for leadership reflection and sensemaking. Study results show that the co-design process functioned as a form of leadership learning, supporting shifts in how the leader made sense of organizational conditions and approached evidence-informed decision-making. title: Academic engagement and faculty participation in higher education strategy-making: evidence from Colombia
abstract: Introduction Higher education institutions are increasingly expected to connect knowledge production with social, organizational, and productive demands while making their strategic processes more open, participatory, and responsive to external environments. Although academic engagement has been widely examined as a mechanism for knowledge transfer and university–industry collaboration, less is known about whether externally engaged faculty members become more able to participate in university strategy. This study addresses this gap by examining academic engagement as a relational pathway through which faculty members’ interaction with external actors may strengthen strategy participation in higher education. Methods Drawing on open strategy and institutional logics perspectives, this study developed and tested a conceptual model linking access to in-kind resources, individual learning, organizational culture, organizational leadership, academic engagement, and strategy participation. A cross-sectional survey was administered to 147 full-time faculty members at a Colombian higher education institution. title: Unequal coexistence: governance lock-in among academic mission logics in a multidisciplinary faculty
abstract: This study examines how centralized faculty governance shapes the relative influence of different academic missions in a multidisciplinary university faculty. It focuses on two locally expressed academic mission logics: a research-oriented mission logic and a professional-education mission logic associated with a business school. Based on a single-faculty qualitative case study and a bounded analytical corpus of 43 governance documents selected from a broader archive of 186 documents produced between 2009 and 2024, the study traces how these logics were expressed, evaluated, and translated into organizational decisions. The analysis identifies four interconnected governance processes: representational asymmetry, agenda formation, leadership-background continuity, and allocation and evaluation. These processes structured access to decision-making arenas, shaped which issues were framed as strategic, influenced the disciplinary experiences represented in leadership and case preparation, and translated strategic recognition into developmental capacity. title: The access–conversion gap across countries: how generative AI adoption exceeds learning use
abstract: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence has diffused rapidly among learners, but a question remains whether that reach becomes useful for learning or stalls at access. This distinction matters most where learners already have connectivity, so the barrier is no longer reaching the technology but converting access into learning use. Methods This study draws on a survey of 14,653 computer science learners across 166 countries, a population for whom first-level access is broadly shared. A two-part model separates whether an everyday user converts to any learning use from how widely converters then use the tool, estimated across World Bank income tiers. Results Everyday adoption is high across income levels and is not lower in poorer settings. The quantity that varies is conversion. Among everyday users, those in low-income countries are markedly less likely to convert to any learning use, at an odds ratio of 0.49 (95% CI 0.27, 0.90), while breadth among converters does not differ by income tier. title: Designing responsible AI feedback in higher education: faculty readiness, student judgement, and metacognitive calibration
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is now part of everyday academic work in higher education, including feedback. However, AI feedback does not automatically lead to learning. It can help students rethink a concept, improve a draft, and notice gaps in their work, but it can also create a false sense of progress when students accept suggestions without understanding them. This Perspective article argues that responsible AI feedback depends on faculty readiness and students’ evaluative judgement. Readiness is not mainly technical. It involves pedagogical judgement: knowing how to design tasks in which students work with feedback, compare it with evidence, revise with purpose, explain their choices, and remain responsible for the final submission. The article focuses on generative AI feedback and uses metacognitive calibration as a central concept. Calibration refers to the relationship between students’ confidence or self-judgement and independently evaluated evidence of performance. title: Refining posthuman aesthetic pedagogy for teacher education through multidisciplinary expert consultation
abstract: Artificial intelligence and digitally mediated creative practices are changing not only the tools available to teachers but also the conditions under which teachers exercise professional judgment. Although posthuman scholarship offers a rich vocabulary for understanding relational agency among humans, technologies, materials, and environments, its educational implications often remain philosophically expansive and pedagogically underspecified. This study therefore refined an initial conceptual framework of Posthuman Aesthetic Pedagogy for teacher education through multidisciplinary expert consultation. The study used a theory-informed qualitative design rather than an inductive theory-generation approach. Five expert fields spanning art education, curriculum studies, educational philosophy, media aesthetics, and contemporary artistic practice critically examined the framework's coherence, educational relevance, conceptual relations, and implications. title: GenAI accelerates surface localization but not deeper culturally responsive teaching in UAE higher education
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping higher education teaching, yet little is known about how faculty in non-Western contexts evaluate and adapt its outputs for culturally responsive teaching (CRT). This qualitative interpretivist study examined how faculty in UAE higher education used GenAI to support cultural responsiveness while navigating local norms, institutional expectations, and ethical constraints. Drawing on Gay's CRT framework, we conducted semi-structured interviews with 20 faculty members across disciplines and national backgrounds. Thematic analysis identified four themes: culturally responsive pedagogical strategies; faculty sensemaking; cultural and relational benefits; and institutional, ethical, and cultural risks. Findings suggest that GenAI helps faculty localize examples, language, and materials more efficiently, but this does not necessarily produce deeper culturally responsive teaching. Responsiveness depends on whether faculty critically examine bias, representation, and whose knowledge is prioritized. title: A Culturally Responsive Digital Differentiated Learning framework is associated with greater engagement and narrower learning disparities in higher education: a quasi-experimental mixed-methods study
abstract: Background Engagement and achievement gaps in higher education remain persistent, especially for students from lower socioeconomic and minority cultural backgrounds in digital learning environments. Objective This study examined whether participation in LMS-based courses implementing a Culturally Responsive Digital Differentiated Learning (CR-DDL) Framework was associated with greater improvements in student engagement and learning outcomes and with narrower observed engagement disparities compared with standard LMS-based instruction. Methods An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design was used with 252 undergraduates in public health and agrotechnology programmes at three Indonesian institutions, comparing CR-DDL courses ( n = 129) with standard LMS-based courses ( n = 123). Quantitative data included pre- and post-intervention Higher Education Student Engagement Scale scores, LMS-derived behavioural indicators, and final course scores. Outcomes were analysed using linear mixed-effects models with a random intercept for course to account for the clustering of students within the six participating course clusters. title: GenAI literacy and online learning resilience among Chinese university students: the mediating role of self-efficacy
abstract: Introduction With the rapid spread of GenAI technologies, university students are both empowered by new technological affordances and confronted with multiple challenges in digital learning environments, including technological adaptation, psychological pressure, and cognitive load. Against the backdrop of accelerating digital transformation in Chinese higher education, this study explores how GenAI shapes the online learning resilience of Chinese university students. Methods Drawing on a survey of 306 students from five universities in Xinjiang, this study employs structural equation modeling to examine the impact of GenAI literacy on online learning resilience and to test the mediating role of self-efficacy. Results The results show that GenAI literacy has a significant positive effect on students' online learning resilience, with self-efficacy playing a partial mediating role in this relationship. Specifically, all four dimensions of GenAI literacy —cognitive awareness, usage ability, evaluation ability, and ethical awareness —enhance students' online learning resilience by strengthening their self-efficacy. title: When hybrid (ChatGPT and teacher) feedback does not outperform teacher-only feedback: evidence from A2 EFL writing in Ecuador
abstract: This study investigated whether hybrid (ChatGPT-generated and teacher-provided) feedback could yield greater gains in grammatical accuracy than teacher-only feedback among on-site A2-level English as a foreign language (EFL) students at a technical higher education institute in Quito, Ecuador. A six-week quasi-experimental study involved 41 students from two intact classes: teacher-only ( n = 18) and hybrid feedback ( n = 23). Both groups completed six handwritten writing tasks. Initial feedback was provided in English by the teacher or ChatGPT. Students in both groups reviewed this feedback using the textbook, class notes, and teacher clarification in English and Spanish as needed before rewriting their sentences. All students completed the same 18-item Grammar Accuracy Writing Test before and after the intervention. title: Research foci, design features, and accessibility challenges in digital mathematics and geography textbooks: a scoping review
abstract: Introduction Digital textbooks are becoming increasingly important in mathematics and geography lessons, as interactive and multimedia features that go beyond the capabilities of printed resources are believed to offer particular learning benefits. Despite this growing significance, there has so far been no systematic research review that examines digital textbooks as a subject in their own right in these disciplines. The issue of accessibility, in particular, has been largely overlooked in previous textbook research and has gained particular relevance due to current legislation. This scoping review therefore aims to map the existing literature and to answer three questions: what are the main research foci, which design features of digital textbooks are being investigated, and in what way and to what extent is accessibility addressed. Methods Based on a systematic search in Web of Science and Scopus following the PRISMA-ScR framework, 78 studies (73 in mathematics, five in geography) were included in the final analysis corpus and evaluated using a common coding guide. title: Best practices from a cohort model for underrepresented PhD students in engineering and physics
abstract: The aim of this study is to analyze student satisfaction, outcomes, and best practices for a graduate cohort model that may then be adopted by other institutions. The University of Colorado Boulder (CU) has hosted a Louis Stokes Alliances for Minority Participation Bridge to the Doctorate (LSAMP-BD) program starting with its first cohort supported by the National Science Foundation (NSF) entering in fall 2023. Additional cohorts of affiliated students joined the program in fall 2024 and fall 2025, with support from CU. Internal funding has also supported networking and outreach events, workshops, retreats, and a near-peer mentoring program that pairs 2nd- and 3rd-year students in the program with 1st-year students. Methods employed include surveys and group interviews to assess student satisfaction and analysis of retention data to assess outcomes. Satisfaction with LSAMP-BD programming was rated as high (average score of 4.45 out of 5) by the participants. LSAMP-BD students demonstrated 100% retention in their PhD programs after one year and 91.7% retention after two years. title: Contextual moderation of primary-school achievement gaps: repeated cross-sectional evidence from Luxembourg
abstract: Persistent educational inequalities related to gender, socioeconomic status (SES), and linguistic background remain significant challenges in Luxembourg's education system. Utilizing a repeated cross-sectional design, this study applies multilevel modeling to six annual cohorts (2014–2019) of Grade 3 students to examine whether classroom composition, teacher-student ratios, and a commune-level social index moderate achievement gaps in mathematics and German reading comprehension. Overall, main and interaction effects varied substantially across survey years, demonstrating marked temporal instability. While providing extra resources to disadvantaged communes showed consistent descriptive trends, contextual moderating effects, such as high teacher-to-student ratios or classroom SES homogeneity, were observed only sporadically in isolated years rather than as stable patterns over time. Furthermore, classroom language composition showed no reliable moderating effect across cohorts. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating contextual policy mechanisms across multiple years and caution against drawing sweeping conclusions from single-year snapshot data.

title: Responsive co-agency in educational accompaniment: a relational model integrating agency, personalism, and the pedagogy of alterity
abstract: Educational accompaniment involves helping learners understand their difficulties, participate in decisions, and develop their capacity to act. In tutoring and school–family collaboration, educators must decide how to respect such participation while exercising professional responsibility. This conceptual analysis develops responsive co-agency as an integrative framework for examining those decisions. Its primary scope is adolescent and university education, with explicit limits on its transferability to other developmental contexts. The analysis connects research on agency, autonomy support, and learner engagement with the pedagogy of alterity and Karol Wojtyła's account of personal dignity and participation. A focused comparison with agential realism and an account of ethical answerability clarifies the framework's relational commitments. Four criteria organize the framework: attention to the learner's situation, supported participation in interpretation and action, contribution to shared educational goods, and protection through justice and professional boundaries. title: Growth mindset as an emergent outcome: autonomy and strategy use in second language learning
abstract: Despite growing interest in growth mindset within second language acquisition (SLA) research, mindset interventions have produced consistently modest and context-dependent effects, suggesting that the construct may be theoretically mispositioned. This article proposes a process-oriented framework that reconceptualizes growth mindset not as a stable predictor of achievement but as an emergent outcome of sustained learning experience. The framework conceptualizes growth-oriented beliefs as dynamic and developing dispositions, with learner autonomy and language learning strategies serving as relational and behavioral conditions that shape their development over time. The primary theoretical contribution concerns the role of strategies: rather than treating them solely as performance-enhancement tools, the framework reconceptualizes strategy use as a belief-formation event. title: Reconceptualizing outdoor geoscience learning for the generative AI era: a human-centered instructional model
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) creates a distinctive problem for outdoor geoscience learning: it can broaden questioning and explanation, yet it can also pre-structure what learners notice and displace their interpretation of field evidence. Existing field-learning frameworks explain how conceptual, geographical, psychological, technical, and social novelty shape participation, but they do not fully explain this redistribution of epistemic work and authority. Extending established accounts of technological mediation to field settings, this Hypothesis and Theory article interprets GenAI as an epistemic reorganization of field inquiry rather than as technical novelty alone. It advances the central hypothesis that GenAI is more likely to augment, rather than displace, learners’ epistemic agency when it is introduced after direct observation and an initial learner interpretation, restricted to generating questions and candidate explanations, and subjected to human adjudication against field evidence. title: Bridging the performance gap: the predictive role of leadership support in Tanzanian secondary schools
abstract: In Tanzania, the persistent challenge of low academic achievement in secondary schools has been linked to underperforming teachers, prompting a need to investigate the organisational factors that predict educator effectiveness. This study examines whether leadership support from heads of schools, particularly decision-making involvement, recognition, role modelling, and managerial support, predicts teachers' work performance. Using an explanatory research design and quantitative approach, data were collected from 380 teachers in Iringa and Njombe regions, with 378 valid responses analysed. Regression analysis using SPSS version 27 assessed the strength and significance of relationships between leadership support and teacher performance. Findings revealed a statistically significant positive relationship between overall leadership support and teacher performance. title: Heads of department's networking in academic institutions: the enablers, benefits and disenablers
abstract: This study was conducted to ascertain the extent of heads of department’s networking in a university, with a view to filling a gap in the literature and contributing to practice. The qualitative study employed phenomenology as its research design to explore the lived experiences of heads of department regarding their contacts, connections, and collaborations with colleagues in relation to their administrative duties. The study was underpinned by the Social Network Theory. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 17 heads of department at a university in Ghana. The findings revealed that the heads of department engaged in some level of networking, made possible through the execution of faculty activities such as serving on committees and boards and performing assigned duties together. The relatively strong network among the heads of department appeared to aid them in gaining insightful knowledge, information, and problem-solving acumen for their administrative practice and professional growth and development. title: Organisational conditions for educator wellbeing and sustainable teaching
abstract: Educator wellbeing is widely understood as multidimensional, arising from the interplay of personal experiences, workplace relationships, organisational arrangements, and wider systemic influences. However, interventions often continue to emphasise individual coping, resilience, and stress management, with limited attention to how educators’ work is structured and supported. This paper considers how systemic understandings of wellbeing can inform more sustainable ways of organising teaching. Through a narrative review and integrative conceptual synthesis, it brings together scholarship on teacher wellbeing, emotional labour, workplace inclusion and belonging, psychological safety, and professional agency. The synthesis develops three propositions. The first concerns recognising and supporting the emotional labour embedded in educators’ professional responsibilities. The second identifies workplace inclusion, expressed through belonging, recognition, and equitable participation, as integral to wellbeing. The third highlights the role of psychological safety and professional agency in enabling educators to express uncertainty, exercise judgement, seek support, and influence decisions

title: Online hate speech against the Mapuche people: pre-service history teachers’ educational responses to a teaching scenario
abstract: Introduction Hate speech directed against the Mapuche people, historically perpetuated through the media's mechanisms of racialisation, has found a powerful platform for amplification on social media. This article analyses how trainee how history teachers conceptualise this phenomenon from a pedagogical perspective and what analytical and pedagogical strategies they employ to address it in the classroom. Methods A qualitative-interpretative approach was adopted, using an integrated case study design, in which each of the 22 written responses from trainee history teachers at a university in southern Chile constituted a unit of analysis. Participants were selected through purposive sampling from an intact cohort, and their consent was obtained once the coursework had been marked. The analysis combined deductive and inductive coding, carried out independently by two researchers, with discrepancies resolved through discussion and, where necessary, through the arbitration of a third party. title: A multifactor model for assessing programming knowledge based on the synchronization of AI analytics and expert evaluation
abstract: Introduction The widespread adoption of generative AI tools has created new methodological challenges for the validity of assessment in higher education. If a neural network can write code, how can a student's actual knowledge be assessed objectively? This study proposes a multifactor AI-assisted assessment model for the fair evaluation of AI-supported learning practices in programming courses and examines its alignment with instructor assessment. Methods The study involved 187 undergraduate students from three universities in Kazakhstan. In Phase 1, student submissions were evaluated using a traditional one-dimensional approach focused on functional correctness, and the results produced by instructors and by three large language models (GPT, Claude and Gemini) were compared. In Phase 2, a multifactor assessment model incorporating functional correctness, explanation quality and AI-use level was introduced, and the same submissions were re-evaluated with all three models. abstract: Peace education increasingly requires creative, collaborative, and future-oriented approaches that move beyond teacher-centered moral instruction. In a world shaped by geopolitical conflict, cultural polarization, social inequality, forced migration, digital misinformation, and rapid technological change, students need learning experiences that enable them to interpret, imagine, negotiate, and communicate peaceful possibilities. Although art-based education has been associated with empathy, emotional expression, intercultural understanding, and dialogue, existing discussions often treat art education, peace education, learner agency, peer collaboration, and digital learning as separate areas of inquiry. This Conceptual Analysis article addresses this gap by proposing the Art-Based Multi-Gogy Peace Education Framework as a future-oriented model for peace education in the era of Education 6.0. title: “It didn't just feel like translation”: Saudi EFL learners’ perceptions of translanguaging vs. English-only written corrective feedback
abstract: Introduction Although pedagogical translanguaging has gained increasing attention in multilingual education, little is known about how learners perceive teacher-provided translanguaging written corrective feedback (WCF) compared with conventional English-only WCF. Methods This mixed-methods study investigated the perceptions and experiences of 60 first-year Saudi EFL university students who received either translanguaging or English-only WCF in their English for Specific Purposes writing classes. Data were collected through post-intervention questionnaires ( n = 55) and focus-group interviews ( n = 8) and analysed using descriptive statistics, Mann-Whitney U tests, and thematic analysis. Results Students who received translanguaging WCF perceived it as significantly easier to understand and apply than English-only WCF. title: 360° video presentations, professional vision, and cognitive-affective experience in physical education teacher education
abstract: Introduction Using videos to develop professional vision is a commonly used tool. In recent years, 360° videos have gained increasing popularity, and their impact on knowledge acquisition has been the subject of growing research interest. Therefore, this study investigates how different 360° video presentation formats support the development of professional vision and cognitive-affective processes in prospective physical education (PE) teachers. title: ChatGPT as an AI-based assessment method in library information science education: investigative study in the information studies department
abstract: Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly the emergence of generative tools such as ChatGPT, have intensified scholarly debate regarding their implications for teaching, learning, and assessment in higher education. While existing research has largely emphasized AI-driven automation of pedagogical processes and learning outcomes, limited attention has been paid to the systematic integration of generative AI as a formal assessment mechanism. This study examines the state and use of ChatGPT as an AI-based assessment tool within the Information Studies Department at Sultan Qaboos University. Despite the growing prevalence of AI technologies, many higher education institutions remain cautious in their adoption for assessment purposes, with some categorizing their use as academic misconduct or plagiarism. Such hesitancy reflects unresolved ethical concerns, academic integrity challenges, and the absence of coherent institutional frameworks to guide responsible implementation. title: AI literacy development among special education graduate students: a mixed-methods exploration
abstract: This mixed-method exploratory study examined the development of AI literacy among ( N = 19) master's-level special education graduate students as they explored the integration of generative AI tools to support students with high-incidence disabilities. Participant responses were examined to identify perceptions of AI, intended uses of generative AI, and considerations related to responsible implementation in special education settings. Findings revealed a conceptual shift in participants' perspectives, from viewing generative AI primarily as an administrative tool for increasing efficiency to recognizing its potential as an adaptive instructional scaffold. Participants increasingly emphasized the need for critical human oversight, FERPA compliance, data privacy, and individualized alignment between AI-generated resources and students' educational needs. Intentional AI literacy development can support future special educators in moving beyond basic technical proficiency toward the critical judgment needed to evaluate and implement generative AI responsibly. title: The disclosure gap: why mandating AI transparency without protecting honesty is a leadership failure
abstract: Universities and journals have answered generative artificial intelligence (AI) with one main instrument: mandatory disclosure. Ask researchers to declare what they used, and transparency should follow. The evidence says it does not. Across 5,114 journals and 5.2 million papers, about 70% of journals now require disclosure, yet only around 0.1% of papers published since 2023 declare AI use, and journals with policies show no less AI adoption than journals without them. Submission data from two major publishers tell the same story: 5.7 and 3.3% disclosure, against surveys where between 28 and 76% of researchers say they use these tools. This Perspective argues that the gap is not a compliance failure to be fixed with firmer rules. It is what happens when institutions ask people to volunteer information that carries a real cost, and then do nothing about that cost. Experiments show that AI users are judged less competent and less motivated; researchers have named the effect AI shaming and the punishment of honesty. title: A universal musical minimum: capability, universal design and body percussion in Spanish primary music education
abstract: Music is affirmed as an entitlement across the European Union, yet what children receive varies with the resources their schools and regions can command. This paper applies Universal Design for Learning at a level where it is rarely employed: not the individual lesson, but the statutory curricular minimum itself. Taking Spain as a case study, it examines what minimum of musical participation a state could guarantee in a form from which no school and no learner could be excluded. Joining universal design with the capability approach, the article argues that such a minimum must be defined as a capability rather than as a resource and specified in competencies rather than materials or gestures. It proposes an instrument-independent curricular floor: a legally protected minimum of rhythmic, ensemble-based and improvisatory participation achievable with the body and voice alone, complementary to instrumental provision and never a substitute for it. title: The problem posing capacities of pre-service post-primary mathematics teachers: insights from an Irish university
abstract: In Ireland and internationally, problem-solving is central to post-primary mathematics curricula. Enacting problem-solving in the classroom is challenging: it requires teachers to select or create problems appropriate to their students and the intended (mathematical thinking) learning outcomes. Despite the centrality of problem-solving in curricula in Ireland, post-primary students score higher in procedural tasks than problem-solving in the international assessments. Coinciding with this, in Ireland there is a reliance on textbooks with many tasks requiring low levels of cognitive demands. Combining these findings, there is an onus on teachers to be able to pose mathematical problems to expose students to problem-solving opportunities. This study investigates the problem posing capacities of two cohorts of pre-service post-primary mathematics teachers (PSMTs) in an Irish university. The participants were undertaking a module focused on mathematical problem-solving, with a focus on its teaching. abstract: Introduction This study examined the relationships between the application of software technologies and the delivery of Business Education content in federal universities in South South Nigeria. Specifically, it determined the individual and joint relationships of Cognitive Artificial Intelligence (AI), Voice on the PowerPoint (VOPPT) lectures, Skillshare and Google Forms with Business Education content delivery. Methods A correlational research design was adopted. The population comprised 306 respondents, and the entire population was studied. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire and analysed using simple and multiple linear regression at the .05 level of significance. Five research questions were answered and five null hypotheses were tested. Results Cognitive AI had a significant positive relationship with Business Education content delivery (R = .574, R² = .330, β = .574, t = 12.235, p < .001). title: Curriculum expectation and classroom reality in manipulative use by JHS mathematics teachers in Amansie Central Ghana
abstract: Ghana's Junior High School (JHS) mathematics curriculum expects teachers to use concrete manipulatives. In the Amansie Central District, Basic Education Certificate Examination (BECE) mathematics failure rates exceeded 55% each year from 2022 to 2024; this underachievement provides the context, rather than the object, of the present study. Drawing on a curriculum-enactment perspective, this convergent mixed-methods, cross-sectional study examined JHS teachers' reported use of manipulatives, sources of supply, teaching methods, perceived benefits and challenges, and compared reported use with observed classroom practice. Data were collected through a questionnaire completed by 97 mathematics teachers in 56 public schools, semi-structured interviews with 31 participants, and classroom observations of 16 teachers. Across 13 syllabus topics, between 85.6% and 96.9% of teachers reported using manipulatives, yet only 2 of the 16 observed teachers (12.5%) used them during instruction, a marked discrepancy between reported and enacted practice. title: Teachers’ perceptions of artificial intelligence integration in education: a multi-campus cross-sectional study from Riphah International University, Pakistan
abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into education is accelerating worldwide, yet evidence on teachers’ perceptions remains scarce in the Global South, particularly in resource-constrained Pakistan. This cross-sectional study examined teachers’ perceptions of AI integration at Riphah International University, Pakistan. A 14-item Likert-scale questionnaire was administered to 270 in-service teachers (86.7% male, 13.3% female) across BS Undergraduate through PhD levels. Guided by a proposed Dual-Lens conceptual framework treating perceived benefits and risks as coexisting dimensions, the instrument assessed pedagogical advantages and structural concerns of AI. Descriptive analysis revealed a moderately favorable overall perception (composite M = 3.40, SD = 0.55). Teachers rated interactivity enhancement (M = 3.81), student enjoyment (M = 3.73), and assessment support (M = 3.72) most favorably, while AI replacing human teachers received the lowest endorsement (M = 2.96). An independent-samples t-test showed no significant gender difference (t(268) = −0.245, p = .807, d = −0.044). title: A model of small group discussion as a teaching - learning reinforcement tool involving the medical students in the Department of Anatomy: a prospective analytical study
abstract: The advancement of medical education technology has changed teaching methods from one-way, didactic lectures to two-way, self-directed, and self-motivated active teaching-learning methods. First-year MBBS students are exposed to small group teaching to learn different aspects of anatomy. An innovative module through small group discussions (SGDs) was implemented as an additional teaching-learning method to highlight the differences with small group teaching (SGT). In SGT, the teacher is the active person, while the students are the passive listeners, whereas in SGDs, students are active participants, and the faculty are facilitators. In the present study, we have evaluated the efficiency of SGDs as a teaching – learning reinforcement tool for medical students in the Department of Anatomy. Aim To determine the effect of the SGD module on the academic performance of medical students in the Department of Anatomy. Materials and methods 150 first-year MBBS students from the 2022 and 2023 academic years. title: Language adaptation among linguistically diverse learners in monolingual schools
abstract: A common language of instruction does not create a common experience of language adaptation. This study investigated students’ perceptions of the effectiveness of instructional, social, and digital practices related to language adaptation. A quantitative cross-sectional survey involved 403 students in Grades 4–12 from seven Latvian public schools. The analysis compared the responses of Latvian-, Russian-, and Ukrainian-speaking learners across nine practices. The social domain received the highest descriptive ratings. Real-life and daily language use were among the most highly rated practices across the three linguistic groups. Ratings varied across the selected practices and linguistic groups. The findings informed a theory-based ecological framework of language adaptation. The framework provides a conceptual interpretation of the observed patterns and intergroup differences.

title: Organizational capacity supporting STEAM implementation in early childhood education: a mixed-methods study
abstract: STEAM education in early childhood settings requires not only teaching and learning resources but also organizational conditions that support their use in educational practice. This study examined resource provision and the broader organizational context associated with STEAM implementation in Lithuanian early childhood education institutions using a sequential mixed-methods design. The quantitative component drew on national survey data from 831 institutions and examined teaching and learning resource provision. The subsequent qualitative component involved open-ended responses from 38 educational leaders from institutions included in the quantitative dataset and explored their perspectives on resources, professional learning, collaboration, leadership practices, and barriers associated with STEAM implementation. The quantitative findings revealed variation in resource provision levels across curriculum areas and resource types. Within “Exploring and Understanding the Environment,” several resources showed provision levels above 70%, whereas the provision level for specialized STEAM laboratory kits was 30.01%. title: Psychometric properties of digital progress monitoring in special education: a COSMIN-guided systematic review
abstract: Introduction Digital progress monitoring is central to data-based decision-making in multi-tiered systems of support (MTSS) and response to intervention (RTI), particularly for students with or at risk for special educational needs, yet existing reviews mainly address reading curriculum-based measurement (CBM) and do not sufficiently synthesize digital, cross-domain, and decision-relevant psychometric evidence. Methods This systematic review followed PRISMA 2020 and used a COSMIN-aligned synthesis of measurement properties. Seven databases were searched; study selection and extraction followed a multi-rater pipeline with consensus adjudication. Results The final corpus comprised 106 studies with a cumulative sample of 774,420 students (median study-level n = 459). Psychometric coverage was uneven: reliability was reported in 67% of studies (55% with strong coefficients, defined a priori as ≥ .80); validity was reported most frequently (86%) but reached strong coefficients in only 33%; responsiveness was reported in 45% and reached strong coefficients in only 8%; classification accuracy was reported in 36% (31% strong). title: Dispositional foundations for AI-mediated learning: evidence from a latent profile analysis of grade-8 students in ICILS 2023
abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) becomes increasingly integrated into education, understanding whether students possess the foundational conditions needed to benefit from AI-mediated learning has become an important educational challenge. This study conceptualizes dispositional foundations for AI-mediated learning as the configuration of ICT self-efficacy, attitudes toward technology and expectations of future ICT use that may support meaningful engagement with AI-mediated learning environments, and examines how these configurations relate to objectively assessed digital competence and to student characteristics. ICILS 2023 contains no measure of AI literacy or AI use, so these are candidate foundations rather than a direct measure of preparedness for AI. Using data from 118,764 Grade-8 students across 35 education systems participating in the International Computer and Information Literacy Study (ICILS 2023), we conducted sampling-weighted latent profile analyses on four internationally comparable indicators. title: Assessing digital competences in higher education teachers: a case study
abstract: Integrating Information and Communication Technologies into higher education demands the incorporation of digital competencies into educators’ professional profile. However, the teachers’ digital competencies require continuous updating in line with emerging technological developments. Educational institutions must establish sound policies to evaluate faculty digital skills and design targeted professional development pathways. This study addresses these needs by investigating the digital teaching competencies of faculty members at a university in Quito, Ecuador, through an explanatory sequential mixed-methods case study design. The primary contribution of this manuscript is a baseline institutional procedure for assessing teachers’ digital competencies. Based on these assessment findings, the study also introduces the Digital Competencies Training Program (DCTP), an institutional professional development initiative. The research was conducted in two phases. In the quantitative phase, the DigCompEdu Check-In instrument was administered to 87.5% of the university faculty. title: Enhancing pre-service teachers' GenAI literacy and teaching self-efficacy through teacher-guided GenAI use: a quasi-experimental study
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly integrated into teacher education, requiring pre-service teachers to develop GenAI literacy and teaching confidence in its pedagogical use. This study examined whether teacher-guided GenAI use was associated with higher posttest GenAI literacy and Teaching Self-efficacy than self-directed use and traditional instruction after accounting for pretest scores. A quasi-experimental pretest–posttest design involved 102 pre-service teachers at a Chinese teacher education college. Data came from a GenAI literacy test, a Teaching Self-efficacy scale, and semi-structured interviews. ANCOVA showed significant overall effects of instructional condition on both outcomes after controlling for pretest scores (partial η 2 = 0.17 and 0.08) No significant differences emerged between the self-directed and traditional groups. Interviews highlighted prompt design, output evaluation, and teaching-related confidence. By combining a test-based literacy measure with a three-group comparison, this study provides preliminary quantitative evidence relevant to distinguishing structured teacher guidance from GenAI tool access alone.

title: The Schutte Self-Report Emotional Intelligence Test in allied health sciences students: reliability, essential unidimensionality, and educational and behavioral correlates: a cross-sectional study
abstract: Introduction Emotional intelligence (EI) is an individual-difference characteristic relevant to how health-professions students learn, cope, and engage with support, making its valid measurement a prerequisite for research on student development in this field. This study examined the psychometric performance and educational and behavioral correlates of the Schutte Self-Report Emotional Intelligence Test (SSEIT) in allied health sciences undergraduates at Kuwait University. Methods In this cross-sectional study, the 33-item SSEIT was administered in English, the language of instruction and assessment at the Faculty, through a confidential online survey. Of 561 responses, 559 remained after duplicate removal and 489 after excluding 70 invariant (straight-line) responders, following the screening pipeline of a companion study on the same administration. Reliability, ordinal confirmatory factor analysis (WLSMV) with bifactor indices, polychoric parallel analysis, split-half validation, and exploratory correlates with Holm correction were examined. title: Theory, practice, and perceived competence: Norwegian PETE students’ reflections on teacher education
abstract: Introduction This study investigates PETE students' perceived competence and their reflections on the contribution of their education program, including potential gender differences and associations between perceived competence and program contribution. Methods In total, 58 of all 61 PETE students at the end of their seventh semester answered the questionnaire, which gives a response rate of 95.1%. Results PETE students report uneven competence across domains, feeling most confident in teaching practical PE and least confident in theoretical sport instruction. They also perceive their program as contributing more to practical teaching, especially at lower secondary level, than to disciplinary knowledge or theory-based teaching. Overall, programs appear to be stronger in developing practical skills than theoretical and subject-specific competence. The results also showed minimal gender differences in perceived competence and program contribution. title: Construction and content validation of an OBE-AI-CED integrated teaching framework for the liquor factory design course in local undergraduate universities: a modified Delphi study
abstract: The digital, intelligent and green transformation of the Chinese baijiu industry has introduced new competency demands for liquor engineering education. The Liquor Factory Design course is a comprehensive upper-level engineering design course for students in the liquor engineering program that combines knowledge of brewing technology, chemical engineering, engineering drawing, brewing equipment, energy-saving and environmental protection, and production management. However, the course in local undergraduate universities still has several problems, such as an unclear design task chain, a lack of authentic engineering contexts, ambiguous boundaries for the use of artificial intelligence, and an assessment approach that focuses too much on the final product rather than the learning process. The above problems may limit the all-round development of students’ engineering design abilities. Given the above problems, this paper builds an OBE-AI-CED integrated teaching system for the Liquor Factory Design course by integrating Outcome-Based Education, Artificial Intelligence and Complex Engineering Design. title: Design of a questionnaire to assess digital competence for employability training
abstract: Introduction Information and Communication Technology (ICT) is a fundamental element in personal and professional development, essential for addressing job instability and reducing the risk of unemployment and social exclusion. Methods This article describes the design and validation process of a questionnaire to assess the digital competence of the population actively searching for work ( Cuestionario de Capacitación Digital de la Población en Búsqueda activa de Empleo - Digital Training Questionnaire for Active Job Seekers- , CDPBAE). The methodology combined qualitative and quantitative techniques, including content validation by nine experts, construct validation via Exploratory Factor Analysis using Principal Components Analysis (PCA), and reliability analysis through Cronbach's alpha on a sample of 572 unemployed individuals. Results The final instrument measures three core dimensions: digital ability, digital attitude, and digital perception. Results demonstrated satisfactory psychometric properties and a good overall internal consistency, with a Cronbach's alpha coefficient of .810.
