title: Technology-enhanced and AI-supported instruction: a meta-analysis of student learning outcomes with implications for writing development
abstract: The increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into education has introduced new paradigms for teaching, learning, and assessment, especially in the development of students’ writing performance. This meta-analysis examines the effectiveness of blended, technology-enhanced, and AI-supported instructional interventions on student learning outcomes. Eleven studies representing 477 participants across primary, secondary, and higher-education settings were synthesized. The included studies represented heterogeneous educational contexts and assessed outcomes such as academic achievement, literacy, vocabulary and language learning, digital literacy, and motivation. Accordingly, the pooled effect represents an overall effect on student learning outcomes rather than a writing-proficiency-specific effect. Studies were identified through ERIC, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar and represented 477 participants across elementary, secondary, and higher-education settings and diverse disciplinary contexts. title: The Schools E-Learning Project: a context-responsive teacher professional development model grounded in a research-practice partnership in remote Papua New Guinea
abstract: Papua New Guinea's National Education Plan (2020–2029) positions teacher professional development (TPD) as a key mechanism for improving the quality of education. Despite this commitment, the provision of TPD in Papua New Guinea (PNG) is challenging due to the remoteness of schools and limited infrastructure. This article reports on an innovative model of TPD founded in a research-practice partnership between an international development agency, Long Term Fund, and university, established in 2020, entitled the Schools E-Learning Project (SELP). The SELP combines localised, ongoing coaching by PNG educational leaders with technology integration to strengthen teacher competence and confidence. The design and evaluation of the initiative are underpinned by a program logic and wrap-around evaluation framework constructed by the research-practice partnership to support the sustainability and scaling of the SELP across remote communities in PNG. A baseline needs analysis identifies teachers’ professional learning needs and contextual challenges, providing empirical grounding for the design and implementation of the TPD model. title: From academic burnout to career withdrawal: the progressive path and intervention strategies of professional identity crisis among medical students
abstract: Professional identity crisis among medical students represents a major challenge in contemporary medical education. In this narrative review, we synthesize its multidimensional determinants and propose a three-stage developmental framework comprising academic burnout, professional identity erosion, and career withdrawal intention. These stages represent a progressive broadening of disengagement, from strain centered on medical training, to destabilization of the professional self, and ultimately to reconsideration of a future in medicine. We further organize intervention strategies at the individual, educational, and social/policy levels according to the major problems arising across these stages. By integrating previously fragmented evidence on burnout, professional identity, and career disengagement, this framework provides a conceptual basis for stage-informed intervention and a testable structure for future longitudinal research.

title: “Figure out who I am as a person and then go from there”: youth insights on humanizing education
abstract: Over the past decade, there has been a surge in mental health challenges among adolescents. While social and emotional learning (SEL) programs are positioned to bolster young people's social, emotional, and academic success and mental health, too few SEL programs center adolescent development in the present context, largely ignoring the realities and needs of Black, Indigenous, and People of Color (BIPOC), LGBTQ2SIA+, and students with disabilities. To fill this gap and need for transformative SEL, we hosted a series of focus groups with fifteen BIPOC middle schoolers to ask what they need to belong and thrive at school, given our belief that the youth most marginalized carry the genius to transform schools for every student. In this paper, we share their insights on how educators can create learning environments that ensure their safety, honor their humanity, cultivate joy, and foster their social, emotional, and academic well-being through transformative SEL and liberatory teaching practices. title: A mixed-methods pilot evaluation of the Sohanjana Antibullying Intervention for educators in Pakistan: knowledge gains, cultural barriers, and module effectiveness
abstract: Introduction Teachers play a vital role in the academic and social development of students. Thus, teachers are being trained to prevent bullying in educational institutions. Despite their success internationally, these training programs are limited in low-income countries such as Pakistan. The Sohanjana Antibullying Intervention is a teacher and peer training program designed specifically for Pakistan. It is the first contextualised antibullying intervention of its kind. This study aimed to evaluate the outcomes of the Sohanjana Antibullying Intervention pilot in improving educators' knowledge and to identify cultural and contextual barriers to learning. Methods In this study, 172 educators participated in eight different online sessions, each lasting 4 hours. A mixed-methods approach was adopted, with quantitative data analysed using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Bonferroni correction, and qualitative feedback examined through thematic analysis. title: Enhancing PISA-aligned argumentation skills of prospective biology teachers through generative artificial intelligence
abstract: Despite scientific argumentation being a fundamental competency of the PISA assessment framework, prospective biology teachers often demonstrate insufficient development in evidence-based reasoning and rebuttal construction skills. Considering the limitations of large-scale implementation of individualized approaches in higher education, this study evaluates the effectiveness of Generative Artificial Intelligence (ChatGPT-4) configured as a “Socratic tutor” in developing argumentation skills among future educators. An 8-week quasi-experimental study involving 124 students from a pedagogical university employed traditional peer discussion methods in the control group ( n = 62), while the experimental group ( n = 62) utilized an AI agent that induced cognitive dissonance regarding socio-scientific issues. Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA) of data obtained through Toulmin's Argument Pattern (TAP) and PISA rubrics confirmed that the experimental group achieved statistically significantly higher overall argumentation quality compared to the control group (F (1,121) = 14.23, p < .001, η 2 = .105). Communication as a catalyst: strengthening literacy through teacher–parent partnerships
abstract: In rural inclusive education, communication between educators and parents transcends logistical necessity; it serves as a transformative catalyst for learners’ literacy advancement. In Foundation Phase classrooms, where learners rely significantly on both home and school contexts, successful communication serves as a conduit for continuous learning support. This article examines the crucial role of communication in promoting literacy among learners with diverse abilities through effective partnerships between educators and parents in inclusive rural schools. Drawing on Epstein's theory, it highlights the importance of trust and mutual respect in fostering collaborative relationships. The study employed a qualitative methodology, including focus group interviews with fifteen Foundation Phase educators and nine parents, to examine the challenges and strategies for effective communication. Findings indicate that consistent, culturally responsive communication has a significant impact on parental involvement and literacy outcomes. title: Perceived stress, dental environmental stress, and academic performance among dental students: a cross-sectional study
abstract: Objectives This study investigated perceived stress and dental environmental stress among dental students, their relationships with academic performance, and the potential association of participation in the Integrative Mind-Body Wellness Initiative (IMBWI) with students’ well-being and academic outcomes. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted among dental students at the UCLA School of Dentistry. Participants completed the Perceived Stress Scale (PSS-10) and the Dental Environment Stress (DES) questionnaire, along with self-reported demographic and academic measures, including academic performance. Regression analyses were performed to identify factors associated with stress outcomes and academic performance. Spearman's correlation analysis was used to evaluate associations between stress scores and academic performance, with statistical significance set at p < 0.05. Results Mean (SD) PSS and DES scores were 21.64 (6.74) and 58.03 (15.53), respectively, indicating moderate stress levels. title: Media literacy as pedagogical practice: preparing secondary teachers to foster critical engagement with aggressive media portrayals
abstract: Teacher education offers little guidance on how teachers might be prepared to support adolescents’ critical engagement with aggressive media portrayals. This study examines how media literacy was constructed as a pedagogical practice by 30 secondary school teachers in Kerala, India, a regional context in which cinema carries considerable cultural weight, across an eight-session professional learning (PL) sequence extending over one academic year. A longitudinal mixed-methods intervention design was adopted, combining an embedded qualitative strand generated during the sequence with a sequential explanatory strand that followed the post-test. Pre- and post-intervention surveys measured teachers’ beliefs about adolescents’ analytical capacity and their self-efficacy for facilitating critical media analysis, while session artefacts, reflective journals, stimulated-recall dialogues and post-intervention interviews were used to trace changes in pedagogical reasoning. title: Financial literacy in digital and AI-supported educational contexts: a bibliometric and PRISMA-based systematic review
abstract: In an era of expanding digital finance, fintech innovation and AI-supported decision-making, financial literacy has become a critical educational priority for informed, inclusive and responsible participation in contemporary financial systems. This study examines financial literacy in digital and AI-supported educational contexts through bibliometric mapping and a PRISMA-based systematic review. A bibliometric analysis of 3,105 Web of Science and Scopus records identified the broader conceptual structure of the field, followed by thematic synthesis of 29 studies with educational relevance. Methodological quality was assessed using design-specific JBI Critical Appraisal Tools. The findings show that financial literacy and financial inclusion form the main conceptual hubs, while fintech and digital finance act as bridging themes. AI-related research is visible, but is mainly linked to prediction, decision-making, fintech adoption and digital services rather than direct pedagogy. title: Assessing what counts: findings from a grade 1 mathematics national diagnostic assessment in Lebanese public schools
abstract: Introduction This study examines performance in Lebanon's 2025 National Diagnostic Assessment (NDA) in Grade 1 mathematics, administered by the Ministry of Education and Higher Education (MEHE) across public schools. The assessment evaluated student performance in Natural Numbers, Addition and Subtraction, and Geometry using 29 scored items, with Geometry represented by a single item. Methods Data from 18,418 students across 818 public schools were analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics, supplemented by school-clustered mixed-effects models to account for the nested structure of the data. Results The overall mean score was 15.62 out of 29 (53.9%), below the MEHE 60% threshold. At the domain level, 45.4% of students were classified below the defined proficiency threshold in Natural Numbers and 61.6% in Addition and Subtraction; the corresponding figure for Geometry was 51.9%, based on its single-item measure. Item-level results identified weaknesses in areas including place value, multi-digit addition, and missing-addend reasoning. title: Enhancing manufacturing processes through control education with MIT FrED platform
abstract: The transition toward advanced and digitalized manufacturing requires engineers and technicians who can connect control-theory concepts with the practical implementation, validation, and troubleshooting of feedback systems. However, control education and industrial training often address modeling, simulation, controller design, and hardware implementation as separate activities, limiting learners’ opportunities to experience the complete control-engineering workflow within a realistic manufacturing context. To address this gap, this paper presents an educational and industrial training framework based on the Fiber Extrusion Device (FrED), developed at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), and structured according to the V-model. The framework integrates (1) process analysis and performance specification, (2) modeling and system identification, (3) controller design and simulation, (4) hardware implementation, and (5) results evaluation and discussion. title: Digital translation practices in university English learning: adoption, disciplinary variation, and AI-assisted revision
abstract: Introduction Machine translation and generative artificial intelligence (AI) are now common resources in English as a foreign language learning, yet evidence from Latin American higher education remains limited and often conflates tool use with learning impact. This study characterized translation practices, tool preferences, print-dictionary use, and AI-assisted text revision among university students in southern Peru. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 435 students from 37 degree programs and seven faculties at a public university. Questionnaire items were analyzed as separate indicators rather than combined into a latent scale. Valid percentages with 95% Wilson confidence intervals were estimated, paired exact McNemar tests were used for within-participant comparisons, faculty differences were assessed using Monte Carlo chi-square tests with false-discovery-rate adjustment, and an exploratory logistic regression was fitted. title: An interventional study on enhancing print awareness in senior kindergarten children through gamified picture book teaching
abstract: Print awareness, encompassing children's understanding of the functional, formal, and rule-based aspects of written language, is a critical precursor to early literacy. Despite growing interest in picture-book interventions, few studies have systematically examined classroom-based gamified approaches to enhancing print awareness among Chinese kindergarten children. This study investigated the effects of a six-week gamified picture book intervention on print awareness within the Chinese logographic writing system. Fifty senior kindergarten children (aged 5–6 years) from two intact classes in an urban kindergarten in China participated in the study. Using cluster randomization at the classroom level, one class was assigned to the experimental group ( n = 25) and the other to the control group ( n = 25). Children in the experimental group participated in weekly gamified picture-book activities, whereas those in the control group received regular picture-book instruction. Print awareness was assessed before and after the intervention across three dimensions: Print Function, Print Form, and Print Rules. title: Through the Kaleidoscopic Lens of Art: a STEM education pathway within Italy’s PCTO framework
abstract: Interdisciplinary approaches can create opportunities for connecting scientific observation with artistic interpretation and environmental communication. The “Kaleidoscopic Lens of Art: Imaging the Environment” project was implemented within Italy's PCTO (Pathways for Transversal Skills and Career Guidance) framework through collaboration between the Art High School “Mario Festa Campanile” (Melfi-Southern Italy) and researchers from CNR-IMIOT (National Reserach Council of Italy - Istituto di Metodologie Integrate per l'Osservazione della Terra). The pathway involved 27 third-year high school students from the Figurative Arts, Architecture and Environment, and Audiovisual and Multimedia tracks and focused on the translation of environmental concepts, geospatial data, and satellite imagery into artistic forms. The pathway combined scientific lectures, field and laboratory activities, visual analysis, conceptual re-elaboration, and artistic production. title: Promoting learners’ right to human dignity: perspectives of school management teams in two South African primary schools in the Ehlanzeni District
abstract: Introduction Human dignity is a foundational constitutional value in South Africa and a core principle underpinning learners’ rights in education. Despite constitutional and legislative protections, learners’ dignity continues to be undermined in schools through bullying, humiliation, discrimination, and punitive disciplinary practices. This study explored how School Management Teams (SMTs) understand and promote learners’ right to human dignity in two South African primary schools. Methods Guided by Human Rights Theory (HRT), the study adopted an interpretive qualitative case study design. Data were generated through semi-structured interviews and document analysis in two public primary schools in the Ehlanzeni District, Mpumalanga Province. Eight SMT members, comprising principals, deputy heads, and departmental heads, were purposively selected. The data were analysed thematically, including cross-case attention to convergence and differences between the two schools. title: Impact of faculty development on teaching practices in higher education: a scoping review
abstract: Introduction Faculty development (FD) is an established feature of Higher Education, yet its impact on what teachers actually do in their teaching has been studied less often than outcomes such as satisfaction, learning and attitudes. This behavioural level is the third of the four outcome levels in the adaptation of Kirkpatrick's model developed for FD in Higher Education. No prior review has mapped it across disciplinary fields outside health professions education, and the present scoping review addresses that gap. Methods Following the PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews, we included empirical and theoretical sources published in English between 2005 and 2025 that reported a change in the teaching practices of university teachers following structured FD, in any discipline other than health professions education. Scopus and Web of Science were searched, with the last search on 25 April 2026. Three reviewers charted the data independently, coding the evaluation framework, the assessment method and type of evidence, and the indicator and direction of effect. The teaching-research nexus under pressure: sustaining ideals in uneven and changing times across disciplines
abstract: Professors in higher education are commonly expected to combine teaching and research, yet the relationship between these activities remains contested. This article explores how professors make sense of the teaching-research nexus in their everyday academic work. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with 16 professors in philosophy, mathematics, law and medicine at two Norwegian research-intensive universities, we explore professors' meaning-making with particular attention to the dialectical process between academic experiences and institutional structures. Framed by mundane phenomenology, we find the nexus to be a core element of the academic role and central to how professors understand academic work. The combination of teaching and research is sustained through professors' understanding of the role as interconnected engagements within their disciplinary fields. Research deepens teaching, and teaching can generate reflection, questions and, at times, new research ideas. title: A dynamic pyramidal model of teaching excellence in higher education: a critical analytical reflection
abstract: Teaching excellence in higher education is often conceptualized through isolated dimensions such as instructional quality, assessment practices, or technological integration. However, these approaches may overlook the dynamic and interdependent nature of educational processes. This study presents a critical analytical reflection aimed at synthesizing high-level evidence and proposing an integrative conceptual model of teaching excellence. An interpretative synthesis was conducted using 35 high-level studies (systematic reviews, meta-analyses, umbrella reviews, and scoping reviews) published between 2015 and 2025, complemented by five international policy reports. The analysis followed a thematic and iterative approach supported by an analytical matrix, coding procedures, and conceptual triangulation. The findings reveal convergence across five interrelated dimensions: teacher–student interaction, higher-order cognitive processes, pedagogical strategies, formative and authentic assessment, and digital technologies. title: Artificial intelligence as academic infrastructure: governance, administrative intelligence, and AI fluency in Kazakhstan’s higher education sector
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly part of higher education's institutional infrastructure, extending beyond teaching and learning to governance, administration, and student support. This study examines how AI Governance Readiness (AIGR) influences Administrative Efficiency through AI (AEAI), AI Fluency Orientation (AIFO), and Student Retention Intentions (SRI), while assessing the mediating roles of AEAI and AIFO and the moderating role of Equity Perception (EPS) in Kazakhstan's higher education sector. Drawing on Dynamic Capability Theory and Sociotechnical Systems Theory, the study develops and empirically tests an institutional capability model using 935 valid responses from students, faculty, academic administrators, and digital administration staff across public and private universities. The scholars analyzed the data using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS 4.0, supported by RStudio. The measurement model demonstrated satisfactory reliability, convergent validity, and discriminant validity, while the structural model showed adequate explanatory and predictive performance. title: Rethinking AI integration in African higher education: a mixed-methods investigation of capacity, equity, and governance across sub-Saharan Africa
abstract: The Revolutionizing Tertiary Education for Africa's Thriving AI Economy and Workforce (RetAIn) project presents a comprehensive, multi-method investigation into the conditions, constraints, and catalysts shaping Artificial Intelligence (AI) adoption across African Higher Education Institutions (HEIs). Deploying both qualitative multi-stakeholders Focus Group Discussions (FGDs) from three African countries (Ghana, Rwanda, Namibia) and a quantitative cross-country survey across five Sub-Saharan African nations (Ghana, Rwanda, Namibia, Kenya, and Zambia), this study produces a richly triangulated account of AI integration dynamics on the continent. The FGD strand revealed a stark divergence in national AI trajectories: Rwanda operates under a strong top-down policy vision hindered by institutional rigidity; Namibia exhibits pragmatic institutional adaptability constrained by geographic and economic smallness; and Ghana demonstrates emergent, bottom-up innovation within a national policy vacuum. title: Future proofing the academy: the nexus between stakeholder support and academic staff performance
abstract: Evidence suggests that academic staff in Nigerian public universities are under-supported in ways that directly undermine the delivery of Sustainable Development Goal 4. Previous research has established that stakeholder engagement matters for educational quality, but only a few empirical studies have tested the specific institutional mechanisms through which this engagement produces performance outcomes in resource constrained African higher education systems. To date, studies have not examined how training and development programmes function as an institutional bridge between training and development plans and academic staff performance in this context. This study set out to investigate the extent to which stakeholder support drives academic staff performance, specifically highlighting how institutional training and development initiatives serve as the crucial bridge for this impact. Grounded in Stakeholder Theory and Social Exchange Theory, the study tests four hypotheses using a quantitative design. title: Scaffolding-based differentiated instruction and students’ algebra achievement: evidence from mathematical understanding and problem-solving performance
abstract: Introduction This study examined scaffolding-based differentiated instruction and students' algebra achievement and perceptions. Methods A quantitative quasi-experimental design involving 120 students was employed. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics and ANCOVA. Results The experimental group's mean achievement increased from 61 to 75, compared with 60 to 65 in the control group. Students reported moderately positive perceptions (M = 3.423, SD = 0.588). Discussion Scaffolding-based differentiated instruction was associated with improved algebra achievement and offers a potential approach to addressing diverse learning needs.

title: Institutional policies for responsible generative AI use in Saudi higher education: a policy review and gap analysis of national-to-institutional implementation
abstract: Saudi Arabia has established a comprehensive national-level governance landscape for generative artificial intelligence through the Saudi Data and Artificial Intelligence Authority (SDAIA), including the AI Ethics Principles (2023), Generative AI Guidelines (2024–2025), the AI Adoption Framework, and the Saudi Academic Framework for AI Qualifications, alongside broader strategic directions under Vision 2030. This study employed systematic documentary analysis combined with gap analysis to examine eight national-level policy and strategic documents, focusing on governance principles, operational mechanisms, and their relevance to Saudi higher education. title: Conceptualizing truth-telling pedagogies in the Norwegian—Sámi context: beyond “closing the knowledge gap” in teacher education
abstract: This article explores truth-telling pedagogies in the Norwegian - Sámi context in the wake of the 2023 Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC). While the TRC emphasizes shared knowledge as a foundation for reconciliation, it marginalizes explicit engagement with colonialism, thereby risking continued reproduction of sanctioned ignorance and colonial power structures. Placing experiences from research and practice in the Norwegian - Sámi context in conversation with international discussions on truth-telling and decolonial and affective pedagogies, the authors argue that truth-telling must move beyond addressing a perceived “knowledge gap” toward confronting coloniality as ongoing structure. A model for a conceptual framework for truth telling in the Norwegian - Sámi context is suggested and explored. The model constructs truth-telling as emerging through invitations, openings, and the cultivation of discomfort as a collective capacity. The authors argue that while truth-telling pedagogy holds transformative potential and can be an avenue for nurturing anti-colonial hope, depoliticization is a real risk if truth-telling is detached from broader structural change.

title: Operationalizing doctoral persistence: dissertation chairing as a shadow retention system
abstract: Introduction Dissertation chairs play a consequential role in supporting doctoral persistence, yet less is understood about how their work is situated within doctoral education and the institutional capacity available to support it. This study examined how experienced dissertation chairs operationalize persistence during candidacy and what their experiences reveal about the organizational conditions shaping this work. Methods This basic interpretive qualitative study examined the experiences of 20 experienced dissertation chairs representing 12 research-intensive, predominantly White institutions in the United States through semi-structured interviews. Guided by the Intersectional Path-Goal Mentoring Framework (IP-GMF), data analysis consisted of an iterative process of deductive and inductive coding to examine chairs' persistence-supporting practices and the organizational conditions shaping their work. title: Pre-service physics teachers as designers of AI-based pedagogical infrastructure: supporting metacognitive learning in STEM classrooms
abstract: This study explored how pre-service physics teachers design artificial intelligence (AI)-based pedagogical infrastructure to support metacognitive learning in STEM classrooms. A qualitative interpretive design was employed with 30 pre-service physics teachers enrolled in a physics teacher education program at a university in Kazakhstan. Following two preparatory workshops, participants developed, tested, and refined AI-supported STEM lesson scenarios over 12 weeks. Testing involved peer-based micro-teaching with fellow pre-service teachers acting in simulated student roles; no school students participated. Data comprised individual semi-structured interviews, lesson plans, AI interaction scenarios, prompt sequences, and reflective notes and were examined using reflexive thematic analysis. Six interrelated themes were identified: designing AI-supported STEM lessons; supporting metacognitive regulation and formative assessment; aligning AI use with the physics curriculum and STEM objectives; preserving student agency and ensuring responsible AI use; developing teacher design agency; and addressing conditions for sustainable implementation. title: L2 grit and enjoyment as the crucial links between ideal L2 self and willingness to communicate: evidence from mediation and latent profile analyses
abstract: The present study explored the associations among ideal L2 self (ILS), L2 grit, foreign language enjoyment (FLE), and willingness to communicate (WTC) among Chinese EFL learners. It examined the mediating roles of L2 grit and FLE in the link between ILS and WTC, and identified latent learner profiles using L2 grit and FLE as profile-defining indicators. A sample of 249 Chinese EFL learners completed self-report questionnaires. Data were analyzed via structural equation modeling (SEM) and latent profile analysis (LPA) followed by BCH distal outcome analysis. The SEM results showed that ILS was positively related to L2 grit, FLE, and WTC. Both L2 grit and FLE exerted significant mediating effects on the association between ILS and WTC. LPA yielded three distinct profiles: low grit–FLE, moderate grit–FLE, and high grit–FLE. BCH tests revealed significant pairwise between-profile differences in WTC and its subdimensions. WTC exhibited a clear hierarchical gradient across profiles, with the high grit–FLE profile showing the highest WTC, followed by the moderate grit–FLE profile, and the low grit–FLE profile reporting the lowest WTC. The study contributes to positive psychology research

title: Academic stress and its associations with the perceived academic outcomes of pharmacy students: a cross-sectional study
abstract: Introduction Academic stress may affect pharmacy students' academic performance and confidence. This study examined academic stress, coping behaviours, and perceived academic outcomes among pharmacy students at Umm Al-Qura University (UQU). Methods A cross-sectional study included 200 pharmacy students at UQU. A self-administered questionnaire assessed sociodemographic characteristics, academic stress, coping strategies, and perceived academic outcomes. Multivariable regression analyses examined adjusted associations with stress, self-perceived academic performance, and confidence. Results Senior students (Years 5–6) reported significantly higher stress ( β = 4.29, p = 0.001), while higher GPA (3.50–4.00) was associated with lower stress ( β = −2.74, p = 0.022). Common stressors included exam anxiety (66.0%), future career concerns (56.0%), sleep deprivation (53.0%), and heavy workload (50.0%). Physical exercise and seeking social support were most common (41.0% and 35.5%, respectively). title: Organised instruction as a fragile space of minority-language contact: Slovene in Croatia during the COVID-19 pandemic
abstract: Introduction This article examines organised Slovene language instruction in Croatia as an institutionally mediated space of minority-language contact in a context of uneven intergenerational transmission and limited use of Slovene within the family and community. It focuses on the conditions for continuing organised instruction and maintaining learners' regular contact with Slovene during COVID-19-related restrictions. Methods The empirical analysis draws on an online survey conducted among teachers of Slovene in Croatia in 2021 ( N = 18), complemented by a follow-up questionnaire completed by eight teachers in 2026. The follow-up was used as a retrospective qualitative complement, rather than as a second measurement point, to contextualise the 2021 findings through teachers' accounts of pandemic-related disruptions and adaptations. Results The findings indicate that the formal continuation of instruction during the pandemic did not necessarily ensure learners' regular contact with Slovene or sustained opportunities to use the language. title: Does psychology have a truth-telling problem? Survivance as truth-telling pedagogy in psychology education
abstract: Truth-telling and reparative praxis have become central concerns in higher education, particularly in settler-colonial contexts where public institutions have denied, minimized, or excluded histories of violence, dispossession, and exploitation. Psychology education holds a specific responsibility within this work as psychological research, assessment, diagnosis, and practice have participated in colonial projects through racialized theories of intelligence and health, clinical pathologization of systemic harms, extractive research, and training models that position Euro-Western knowledge as universal. Symbolic response and deficit framing limit reconciliation-oriented teaching when institutional language, course content, and professional training leave colonial authority intact or position Indigenous Peoples primarily through harm. This article adapts survivance and health survivance scholarship into a pedagogical framework to guide curriculum design, testimony protocols, case teaching, research assignments, supervision discussions, and assessment in psychology education. title: Navigating dual pathways: learning-oriented and instrumental identities in AI-mediated informal digital learning of English
abstract: Generative AI is increasingly reshaping how learners engage in informal English learning beyond the classroom, making AI-mediated informal digital learning of English (AI-IDLE) an important emerging learning context. Yet research has predominantly focused on intra-personal psychological factors, the social dimensions of learning, particularly how learners construct their social identities in relation to AI, remain significantly underexplored. This qualitative study examines the social identity categories and their construction processes among 12 Chinese university EFL learners engaged in AI-IDLE. Drawing on Social Identity Theory (SIT), data from semi-structured interviews, reflective journals, and AI chat logs were analyzed using thematic analysis. The findings reveal two distinct identity pathways: learning-oriented academic identities, characterized by deep-learning commitment, humble mindset toward AI, and sustained immersion in the student role; and an instrumental identity, organized around a user category defined by transactional engagement, service satisfaction and surface learning approaches. title: Lecturer presence is linked to perceived learning, while pedagogical and technical factors are linked to satisfaction in synchronous hybrid teaching
abstract: Introduction Hybrid teaching, in which students attend lectures either in the physical presence of a lecturer or synchronously via video link from another location, has become increasingly common at multi-campus institutions, yet research systematically comparing student satisfaction and perceived learning in this format remains limited. Methods This study examined synchronous hybrid teaching in an undergraduate Social Work programme delivered across two Swedish campuses, in which the defining difference between student groups was not physical attendance as such, since students at both sites were present in university classrooms, but whether the lecturer taught in person or via videoconference from the other campus. A total of 282 students completed a study-specific questionnaire across three consecutive semesters, assessing overall satisfaction, perceived learning under both lecturer conditions, ability to focus, sense of community, and technical problems. title: Scaffolded English-dominant interaction framework with young A1 EFL learners: an embedded mixed-methods classroom pilot in Ecuador
abstract: Maximizing target-language exposure may increase opportunities for oral practice in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) classroom; however, rigid English-only practices may restrict beginning learners’ comprehension and participation. This classroom pilot study introduced and examined the classroom implementation of the Scaffolded English-Dominant Interaction Framework, which combines comprehensible input, teacher scaffolding, communicative interaction, and progressively independent oral production. A quantitative-dominant embedded mixed-methods design was employed with 30 fourth-grade A1 learners aged 8-9 years at a private school in Ecuador. Participants completed parallel speaking tasks before and after a 12-session intervention. Performance was rated using a three-point analytic rubric addressing reliance on the first language (L1), speech pauses, and hesitations. The qualitative process was obtained from 12 structured teacher reflection journals and analyzed thematically. The median composite score increased from 5 to 8. title: Value and usefulness of theory in teaching and teacher education: perspectives of teacher educators
abstract: Introduction This study examines how teacher educators at universities, teacher seminars, and schools conceptualize and use theory - defined broadly as scientific professional knowledge, including theoretical frameworks, empirical research findings, and evidence-informed orientation - in their mentoring and teaching practices. Method Using a praxeological-sociological approach and documentary method analyses of interview data, we reconstruct the implicit beliefs that guide educators' actions when mentoring pre-service teachers. Results The findings reveal four variations of theory-conceptions, differing markedly in how theory is conceived of, valued, and incorporated in mentoring. Discussion These divergences show inconsistencies across institutional sites of teacher education and may shape the extent to which pre-service teachers can develop theory-informed professional competence. The study highlights the need for targeted professional development for teacher educators and stronger program-level alignment to better integrate theory and practice in practical placements.

title: Digital moral agency in school ethics curricula: from responsible use to epistemic and socio-technical judgement
abstract: Digital technologies increasingly shape the relationships, information environments and institutional systems within which young people exercise moral judgement, yet curriculum responses often separate digital competence from moral education. This study develops the concept of digital moral agency and examines how it is represented across 13 official Maltese Ethics curriculum, syllabus and policy documents published between 2012 and 2026. Using longitudinal qualitative document analysis, we compared successive formulations of the intended curriculum and coded established dimensions of moral agency and practical wisdom alongside inductively identified digital concerns. The analysis shows continuity in reflection, dialogue, responsibility, care, justice and reason-giving, alongside a widening of the contexts in which these capacities are expected to operate. title: Visualizing literary inquiry: a curriculum framework for digital-humanities pedagogy in English literature
abstract: Literature courses commonly use close reading to guide students through individual passages. Because class time is limited and reading must be selective, however, students may find it difficult to observe patterns across an entire work. Drawing on the change of scale associated with distant reading, this article proposes a five-module curriculum framework for using digital text analysis and visualization in English literature teaching. The modules address language and style, thematic language, chapter-level discourse, character relations, and cross-textual comparison. Each module is designed to help students notice a pattern, formulate a literary question, return to relevant passages, and consider how analytical choices shaped what the visualization shows. Demonstrations based on The Scarlet Letter and The Great Gatsby show that materials for all five modules can be prepared using frequency and concordance analysis, chapter trends, a lexical-family heatmap, a character network, and normalized cross-textual comparison. title: Redesigning collaborative teaching for human–AI partnership: a phase-based AI-constraint design principle in higher education
abstract: Generative AI is now a routine presence in higher-education classrooms, shifting the operative question from whether to permit its use toward when and how access should be structured within a learning activity. This paper reports a design-based research programme examining phase-based AI constraints, deliberately restricting AI access to specific phases of a collaborative teaching method rather than permitting or prohibiting it wholesale, as a design principle for structuring human and AI contributions within collaborative learning activities. The wider DBR programme examined AI-augmented designs across six collaborative teaching methods, administered repeatedly to five student groups over two academic years; the phase-based AI-constraint principle reported here as DP1 was developed through, and its evidence anchored in, Think-Pair-Share, with the other five methods contributing broader DBR context rather than independent confirmatory evidence. title: Low-performing students and growing educational inequalities in Finland
abstract: Finland is known worldwide for its good learning outcomes and success in reducing educational inequalities. In this study, we examined trends in educational equality from the perspective of low-performing students in Finland using the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) data from 2003 to 2022. We studied changes in the share of low-performing students in mathematics by gender, socioeconomic status (SES), immigrant background, and the community location of schools using descriptive statistics. In addition, we used logistic regression analysis to study the factors that are associated with low performance in 2012 and 2022. The results showed that the share of low-performing students increased across all groups. Since 2012, the share of low-performing students between girls and boys has begun to diverge. The results also showed a strong difference in performance according to SES, with a marked decline in performance among students with low SES. However, the gap between native and immigrant students narrowed from 2012 to 2022, which is explained by the fact that the share of low-performing native students increased. title: Effects of a gamified intervention on gratitude in a Colombian population
abstract: Gamification promotes the development of competencies in continuing education contexts. This study analyzed the effects of a gamified intervention on gratitude in a Colombian population. A four-condition quasi-experimental design was used (experimental, training, infographic, and no-treatment), with pretest–posttest measurements obtained from 160 participants. The G-20 Gratitude Questionnaire was administered. Analyses using linear mixed-effects models revealed a significant Condition × Time interaction for total gratitude, F(3, 156.0) = 4.83, p = .003, with significantly greater increases in the experimental condition than in the other conditions and effect sizes ranging from medium to large. Significant effects were observed for recognition of gifts ( p = .005) and interpersonal gratitude ( p = .018). The findings provide evidence of the potential of gamification as a pedagogical strategy in continuing education programs, with implications for instructional designers and human resource management professionals.

title: Inclusive inquiry in science education: reframing inquiry-based science education through disability studies in education
abstract: Inquiry-based Science Education (IBSE) is frequently framed as a participatory and therefore inclusive approach to science learning. This paper argues that this claim rests on an under-theorized understanding of participation. Dominant classroom enactments of IBSE embed normative assumptions about epistemic competence, communicative form, and learner autonomy—assumptions that function as selective recognition conditions, shaping who is seen as capable of participating in scientific inquiry, and in what ways. Drawing on Disability Studies in Education (DSE) and its norm-critical tradition, the paper analyzes how these assumptions produce epistemic exclusion. This exclusion arises not through the intentions of individual teachers or the commitments of IBSE as a framework, but through the unexamined norms by which classroom inquiry is organized, paced, and recognized as legitimate scientific practice. title: Practice and dual impact of an undergraduate-graduate collaborative learning model in pharmaceutical education
abstract: Background Traditional hierarchical teaching silos undergraduate and graduate education, hindering cross-level knowledge interaction and students’ comprehensive competency development. How to integrate learners at different academic stages to boost interactive learning and educational quality has long been a difficult issue in pharmaceutical pedagogy. This study constructed and implemented an undergraduate-graduate collaborative learning model to tackle these drawbacks. Methods This study adopted a non-randomized quasi-experimental design with intact classes. Fixed collaborative groups were formed in a Pharmaceutical Botany and Pharmacognosy course to complete a semester-long inquiry-based project. Intervention effectiveness was evaluated via multi-source data, including single-group self-reported questionnaires (intervention group only: n = 42 undergraduates), objective final examination score comparisons (experimental n = 42 vs. control n = 48), and thematic analysis of standardized reflection journals and semi-structured interviews. title: From classroom event to networked visibility: audience amplification and the limits of relational embedding in higher education
abstract: Students' engagement and sense of belonging are increasingly shaped in settings where classroom experience and digital interaction overlap – what Floridi calls the “onlife” condition, in which online and offline life form a single continuum. This article examines one such episode. A well-known Italian influencer took part in the closing session of a university course, and the Department then narrated the visit through its official Instagram and Facebook accounts. We ask whether the visibility that those posts generated and students’ relational participation in the Department's online community are the same outcome or two different ones. title: A computationally-integrated simulation-focused problem-based learning framework for engineering dynamics: design, implementation, and mixed-methods evaluation in an OBE-aligned undergraduate course
abstract: Engineering dynamics courses demand simultaneous development of mathematical modelling, computational implementation, and communication competencies, yet conventional instruction rarely provides authentic contexts for their integration. The primary objective of this study was to design, implement, and empirically evaluate a Simulation-Focused Problem-Based Learning (SF-PBL) framework that integrates first-principles Newtonian and Lagrangian mechanics with Python-based numerical simulation within an Outcome-Based Education (OBE)-aligned curriculum. The framework was embedded within a 15-week undergraduate Dynamic System Modeling (DSM) course ( N = 53, B.Tech Mechatronics Engineering, Semester IV, January–April 2026) at a single NBA-accredited institution in India. It operationalises a four-phase computational pipeline—System Identification, Mathematical Modelling, Computational Simulation, Validation & Communication—scaffolded through an Explain-Try-Challenge (E-T-C) model and assessed via a six-judge external expert panel. title: Neuromyths about motor development and coordination among Hungarian teachers: prevalence and associations with completion of motor therapy training
abstract: Neuromyths—misconceptions arising from the misinterpretation or oversimplification of neuroscientific findings—are common among educators and may influence educational practice. However, neuromyths about motor development and coordination remain relatively underexplored. This study examined the prevalence of movement-related neuromyths among Hungarian in-service teachers, with particular emphasis on whether endorsement differed according to completion of motor therapy training, and explored additional factors associated with incorrect responses. A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 734 Hungarian in-service teachers, including 206 who had completed motor therapy training. Participants completed the 44-item Hungarian Neuroliteracy Questionnaire, of which 13 items addressed motor development and coordination. Descriptive statistics, Mann–Whitney U tests, and ordinal logistic regression were used for analysis. The prevalence of incorrect responses across the 13 statements ranged from 7.6% to 95.8%, indicating that misconceptions about motor development and coordination were common. title: Disruptions in engineering academia: a systematic literature review
abstract: Over the past decade, engineering academia has faced increasing disruptions stemming from global crises, such as the COVID-19 pandemic, and systemic shifts such as digital transformation and evolving labor markets. Despite the increasing prevalence of these disruptions, the literature remains fragmented in its definitions, typologies, and strategies for managing disruption in engineering education. This review investigates how disruptions in engineering academia have been defined, categorized, and managed between 2015 and 2024, with a focus on students, faculty, and institutional systems. Reported in accordance with PRISMA 2020, this systematic literature review searched Compendex and Inspec, accessed through Engineering Village, as well as ERIC and Web of Science. A total of 339 peer-reviewed studies were selected and analyzed using inductive thematic analysis to identify patterns in definitions, disruption types, and management strategies related to academic disruption. Most studies lacked explicit definitions of disruption, though thematic analysis revealed dominant framings of disruption as pandemic-induced shock, tech-driven change, and student experience breakdowns. title: Strategies for widening participation in the biomedical science at London South Bank University—a case study
abstract: Introduction and context Black, Asian and Minority Ethnic (BAME) professionals make essential contributions to UK healthcare, biomedical science research, academia, and the life sciences industry, yet remain underrepresented in senior roles. Three barriers recur: limited access to the discipline, a weak sense of belonging, and few visible role models. This study presents targeted strategies implemented within London South Bank University's Biomedical Science Programme (BMS) to address these barriers at key stages of students' career development journey. Aims This case study had two linked Aims: (1) to describe strategies addressing these barriers, and (2) to examine, through a survey of BMS alumni and students, whether barriers were experienced, whether strategies reached them, and what remained unmet. Methods Initiatives included the Black in Biomed conference, providing role models and networking; STEM workshops for school pupils; and BMS Day outreach, offering hands-on engagement and diverse representation. title: Evaluating learner satisfaction and confidence in a precision agriculture MOOC: a cross-sectional study in Palestinian higher education
abstract: Background Precision agriculture (PA) increasingly requires graduates who can work with sensor-based, geospatial and data-driven technologies, yet access to specialised training remains uneven in many under-resourced higher-education contexts. Although massive open online courses (MOOCs) offer a potentially scalable response to this gap, empirical evaluation of precision-agriculture MOOCs and of MOOC-based learning in Palestinian higher education more broadly remains limited, so evidence on learners' satisfaction and confidence in this specific educational context is needed. Methods This study addresses that gap through a cross-sectional, questionnaire-based evaluation of learners participating in a precision agriculture MOOC developed within the BENEFIT Erasmus+ project for Palestinian higher education; the design does not support causal inference. A questionnaire administered following learners' participation in the MOOC was completed by 62 of 69 invited learners (response rate 89.9%). title: The role of professional learning communities in teacher implementation of problem-based learning in teaching senior high school mathematics
abstract: Problem-Based Learning (PBL) is increasingly recognised as an effective approach for promoting students' critical thinking, problem-solving, and conceptual understanding in mathematics. Although PBL is emphasised in the Ghanaian Senior High School mathematics curriculum, its classroom implementation remains limited, and empirical evidence on the role of Professional Learning Communities (PLCs) in supporting it is scarce. This study examined the extent to which PLCs are associated with teachers' implementation of PBL. An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design was adopted. Data were collected from 86 mathematics teachers and school administrators in three public Senior High Schools using a structured questionnaire (83 valid responses retained for quantitative analysis), followed by semi-structured interviews with 15 teachers. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistics and multiple linear regression, and qualitative data were analysed thematically. title: Land, culture, voice, and economics: an Indigenous land based framework for STEM and agricultural education
abstract: As Tribal Nations explore emerging opportunities in bio-based economies, hemp education offers a meaningful platform for integrating land stewardship, cultural knowledge, community priorities, and workforce development. Yet existing science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) and agricultural education models rarely provide culturally grounded approaches that integrate Indigenous epistemologies, land-based pedagogy, and sovereignty-centered economic development. This article introduces a conceptual Indigenous land-based curriculum framework for culturally grounded STEM and agricultural education, using hemp education as an applied and relational learning context. Grounded in Indigenous research methodologies and guided by a Two-Eyed Seeing orientation, the framework was developed through qualitative conceptual inquiry and iterative synthesis of scholarship on Indigenous epistemologies, culturally grounded STEM education, land-based learning, and community-centered economic development. title: Effectiveness of Medical French training in developing communicative competence among health professional students in Ghana
abstract: This study examined the integration of Medical French into the training of health professionals in Ghana in response to the growing need for effective cross-border healthcare communication within the multilingual ECOWAS region. Despite the increasing relevance of French proficiency for healthcare delivery, professional mobility, and communication with Francophone patients, limited empirical research has assessed the effectiveness of Medical French instruction in Anglophone health professional education. Guided by Stufflebeam's CIPP (Context, Input, Process, Product) evaluation model, the study adopted a quantitative descriptive design involving 176 students from the Schools of Pharmacy, Nursing, Midwifery, and Allied Sciences in a public university in Ghana. Data were collected through a structured questionnaire based on the CIPP framework and analyzed using descriptive statistics. title: Inclusive digital education policies in three European countries: a comparative analysis
abstract: This article explores how inclusive digital education is translated and institutionally embedded in national education policies in Austria, Croatia, and Iceland. Drawing on a comparative case study design, we analyse schooling-related policy documents across four analytical dimensions: equitable access to digital devices, provision of assistive technologies and adaptive learning tools, development of teachers’ inclusive digital competencies, and support for digital skill acquisition among learners with special educational needs (SEN). While all three countries have invested substantially in school digitalisation, the findings reveal that inclusive digital education remains unevenly developed across policy systems. In Austria, fragmented governance, a delayed curricular reform for learners with SEN, and the absence of a codified right to assistive technology limit coherent implementation. title: Changes in general and physics-related professional competence facets of early childhood educators
abstract: Introduction Play-based science learning opportunities are considered a promising approach to strengthening science education in early childhood. Professional development (PD) is increasingly recognized as important in this context, yet empirical evidence on play-based physics PD remains limited. In particular, there is a lack of PD programs addressing play-based science learning, and empirical evidence remains limited regarding how play-based physics PD programs support early childhood educators' general and domain-specific professional competencies. Addressing this gap, the present study examines self-reported pre-post changes in selected professional competence facets within the PhysikSPIEL PD program. Methods Participants ( N = 42) were early childhood educators from Germany and kindergarten teachers from Switzerland, enrolled in the 2024 or 2025 program cycle, each lasting approximately three months. title: Fishbone diagram strategy in algebraic word-problem instruction: senior high school students’ achievement and perceptions
abstract: Algebraic word problems continue to pose significant challenges for senior high school students due to difficulties in interpreting problem statements, identifying mathematical relationships, and applying appropriate solution strategies. This study examined achievement differences between students taught algebraic word problems using the Fishbone Diagram Strategy and those taught using the conventional method and examined students’ perceptions of the strategy. A quasi-experimental pre-test-post-test non-equivalent control group design was employed with 128 Senior High School students, comprising 64 students in the experimental group and 64 students in the control group. The experimental group received instruction using the Fishbone Diagram Strategy, while the control group was taught using the conventional method over six weeks. Data were collected using an Algebraic Word Problems Achievement Test and a perception questionnaire. title: Students’ experiences of supplemental instruction and self-reported academic performance in Physics within the bachelor of radiography and extended curriculum programme
abstract: Introduction Supplemental instruction (SI) in higher education is a co-curricular activity that supports student learning and improves academic performance in high-risk modules at the South African University of Technology. However, there is limited empirical evidence regarding SI and student academic performance in modules such as Physics. This study aimed to examine students’ satisfaction with SI facilitation, differences in self-reported academic performance, and factors associated with performance among students participating in SI in the Physics module of the Bachelor of Radiography (BRad) in Diagnostics and Extended Curriculum Programme (ECP). Methods A quantitative, retrospective, observational research design comparing two sequential self-reported assessment categories among students participating in SI was used. A convenience sample of 183 students was approached from an eligible population of 350. title: A conceptual framework: what is impactful learning? A case study of teaching organic chemistry for pre-medical students
abstract: Organic chemistry occupies a contested place in pre-health education: required of nearly all premedical students, experienced as difficult, and justified on grounds that it “teaches you to think”, a claim too vague to evaluate or teach toward deliberately. Existing frameworks do not resolve this tension. This paper adopts a conceptual analysis approach, drawing on Ausubel's rote/meaningful learning distinction and the traditional transfer-of-learning literature, to propose impactful learning as a third pedagogical stage following rote and meaningful learning. Impactful learning is defined as the stage where procedural and reasoning skills exercised in mastering a discipline's content become generalizable cognitive tools deployable outside that discipline. title: A longitudinal evaluation of a university-wide faculty development grant program: pedagogical innovation, student priorities, and programmatic evolution
abstract: Background Faculty development grant programs are strategic levers for improving teaching quality, curriculum design, and student learning, yet longitudinal evaluations remain scarce. In this study, we assess King Saud University's Program for Excellence in Learning and Teaching (PELT)— an early university-wide faculty teaching-grant initiative —examining its implementation, faculty uptake, and programmatic evolution over a decade. Methods Using a longitudinal, multi-source program-evaluation design, we analyzed eight PELT cycles through 157 completed grants, faculty ( n = 108) and student ( n = 413) surveys, and descriptive benchmarking against 11 international peers. Survey data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, and selected faculty ratings were compared using Mann–Whitney U -tests. Results PELT evolved from a high-volume inaugural phase (71 grants) to a more selective model (6–11 grants annually) with a 95.7% completion rate. title: Context sensitivity in ChatGPT–generated peer review: evaluative alignment across positive and negative user-provided contexts
abstract: Introduction Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to support evaluative tasks, raising questions about whether their judgements remain independent when users provide prior evaluative information. This study examined the context sensitivity of GPT-5.5 Instant-generated academic peer-review evaluations under positive and negative user-provided evaluative contexts. Method Sixteen academics evaluated two published manuscripts, classified for the study as relatively higher and lower quality, across four structured conditions. Each participant completed all conditions in separate ChatGPT sessions, yielding 64 peer-review outputs. Descriptive summaries of overall scores and publishability judgements complemented qualitative content analysis. title: Learner autonomy in Ethiopian secondary EFL classrooms: observed teacher practices and student perceptions
abstract: Learner autonomy is widely recognized as a goal of modern language education. However, in Ethiopian EFL contexts, the extent to which autonomy is promoted remains largely unknown. This study investigated the relationship between teachers’ autonomy-supportive practices and learner autonomy in Ethiopian secondary school EFL classrooms, a context marked by large classes, teacher-centered instruction, and exam-driven curricula. Employing an explanatory sequential mixed methods design with quantitative priority (QUAN→qual), the research involved 412 students and 34 teachers from eight public schools in Gurage Zone, Central Ethiopia. Data were collected through classroom observations (Teacher Autonomy-Supportive Practices Observation Schedule, TAPOS), student perception surveys (Student Perception of Autonomy Support Scale, SPASS), and a learner autonomy inventory (Learner Autonomy Inventory, LAI). abstract: Introduction Progression through educational milestones and inequality need not change in parallel: group differences may narrow at one transition, widen at another, or shift into differentiated pathways. Methods Using Romanian administrative records, we compared the 1999, 2004, and 2009 birth cohorts across six transition-specific analyses in two overlapping historical windows. abstract: Objective of the study This study examines the influence of artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled applications on the management and digitalization of higher education institutions, focusing on Pedagogical Enhancement, Data-driven Insight, and Administrative Effectiveness. abstract: Introduction Scientific research has transformed universities; however, in countries such as Peru, gaps in knowledge production persist, making it necessary to strengthen research training and promote evidence-based practices. This study aimed to determine whether attitude toward scientific research and academic self-efficacy statistically predict self-perceived research skills among students at a private university in Peru. Methodology The study employed a quantitative approach with an explanatory–associative scope and a non-experimental, cross-sectional design. A non-probability convenience sampling method was used, and data from 650 university students (52.8% female and 47.2% male) were analyzed. The variables were measured using the Attitude toward Scientific Research Scale (EACIN-R), the Academic Self-Efficacy Scale, and a scale of self-perceived research skills. title: ICT-driven mathematical modelling approaches for embedding education for sustainable development in mathematics teacher education: a systematic review
abstract: This systematic review synthesises evidence on ICT-driven mathematical modelling strategies for embedding Education for Sustainable Development (ESD) in mathematics teacher education. Following PRISMA guidelines, we searched AI-powered, Google Scholar (Google Scholar Labs) (2016–March 2026) and identified 18 peer-reviewed studies that met the inclusion criteria. abstract: Introduction This study investigates the relationship between the L2 motivational self-system and attitudes toward AI-enhanced second language (L2) learning, and tests whether intrinsic and extrinsic motivation mediate these relationships among students learning Chinese or English as a foreign language in Thailand, Macau, and Mainland China. Methods Questionnaire data were collected from 361 participants. Correlational analysis, hierarchical regression, and a bootstrapping approach were used to test mediational relations. Results Both the ought-to L2 self and the ideal L2 self were significantly associated with attitudes toward AI-enhanced L2 learning, with the ideal L2 self showing the stronger association. title: Recognition and power relations in the supervision of school principals
abstract: This conceptual analysis article examines the supervision of school principals through the paradigms of recognition and power relations. Using a comparative education approach, it examines three illustrative governance contexts: the United States, Abu Dhabi in the United Arab Emirates, and the People's Republic of China. Principal supervision is a critical site where leadership of recognition intersects with power dynamics. It is argued that although principal supervision is performed in the name of accountability and, to varying degrees, decentralization of educational administration, supervision structure and practice inextricably reproduce institutionalized power relations. abstract: Educational disengagement (ED) in upper-secondary education is theoretically associated with adolescent social integration and delinquency risks. Using annual provincial data from Shandong Province, China, from 2014 to 2025, this study develops a framework linking education policy reform, ED, and juvenile justice involvement. An interrupted time-series (ITS) design was employed to evaluate the immediate and trend effects of the 2020 upper-secondary education policy reform on ED rates, followed by exploratory regression analyses examining the association between ED and juvenile justice involvement. title: Gamified flipped learning and the affective domain of language learning: a qualitative case study of online English classes
abstract: Gamification and flipped learning have each been linked to enhanced learner engagement, but qualitative accounts of their combined, semester-long use in online language classrooms remain scarce, particularly in Indian higher education, and the affective domain is rarely examined as a central construct in its own right rather than as a by-product of achievement studies. abstract: Introduction Adverse childhood experiences can negatively affect students' development and classroom functioning, highlighting the need for supportive school environments. This study evaluated teacher-level outcomes of a school-wide trauma-informed approach in eight Dutch mainstream primary and primary and secondary special education schools. title: Beyond tuition-free higher education: financial stress, student sustainability, and persistence-related vulnerability in Ecuador
abstract: Tuition-free higher education reduces a major barrier to university access, but it does not eliminate the indirect financial and material conditions required to sustain academic participation. This Perspective Article introduces student sustainability as a complementary framework for examining whether students have sufficiently stable financial-material, temporal, family-social, and institutional conditions to maintain an academically viable trajectory. Drawing on Ecuadorian and Latin American literature, the article discusses how transportation, food, connectivity, educational materials, employment demands, and limited access to financial support may generate vulnerability even when tuition is not charged. title: Transformational experiences in higher education: sustainability for educational leaders
abstract: As sustainability and climate adaptation become a necessity in the wake of climate change and natural disasters, K12 school district leaders play a crucial role in its implementation. Preparing schools to support students through a changing climate is a weighty but necessary task that educational leaders face; the effects of climate change on student outcomes is far-reaching and long-lasting. abstract: Introduction This review synthesizes empirical findings on flipped classroom instruction in higher education psychology courses and identifies future research directions. Methods Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, 21 studies published between 2017 and 2024 were identified through Web of Science, Scopus, and citation searching. A narrative synthesis was conducted to examine study characteristics, instructional activities, benefits, and implementation challenges. Results The reviewed studies were mainly based on quantitative quasi-experimental designs. Pre-class video-based materials and in-class collaborative activities were the most frequently reported instructional practices. abstract: As academic researchers find themselves in an increasingly competitive environment with strictly hierarchical power structures, there is growing interest in exploring new forms of leadership in universities. In this article, we discuss how sharing the leadership role in research projects can be a way to lead that follows feminist principles in order to create a supportive work environment where innovative research can happen at the intersection of individual and collective growth. abstract: This study presents a Design-Based Research (DBR) framework integrating Digital Twin development into undergraduate engineering education through Project-Based Learning. abstract: The advent of generative artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming academic production and confronting the social sciences with the challenge of preserving critical thinking in the face of mechanically generated content. This research examines the perceptions and practices of social science lecturers and students at Ecuadorian universities regarding the use of AI, together with their motivations, constraints and the institutional policies currently in force. title: From following to caring and acting: analyzing social media's role in shaping mindsets and transforming habits for sustainable living
abstract: The urgency for sustainable consumption underscores the need to disseminate sustainability knowledge and promote environmentally responsible habits across societies. Due to its broad reach, social media has the potential to promote sustainable consumption by influencing habits and increasing environmental awareness. In this study, we investigate the role of social media through the design and strategic use of an Instagram account, WeSustainQtr, which aimed to disseminate sustainability knowledge and encourage sustainable consumption practices in Qatar and similar settings, through culturally relevant and solution-oriented content. title: Exploring educational involution: a qualitative study of stakeholders’ perspectives in Jiangsu Province, China
abstract: The term “educational involution” has emerged as a prominent societal concern in contemporary China. Involution now characterises an educational phenomenon where students and families invest excessive effort into academic competition yet achieve diminishing returns while experiencing heightened anxiety. Through this exploratory case study, we investigate stakeholders’ perspectives and lived experiences of educational involution in Jiangsu Province through qualitative research, conducting nine in-depth interviews with students, parents, and teachers across primary (Years 1–6), secondary (Years 7–9), and high school (Years 10–12) levels (one participant per role per level), using stratified and convenience sampling across three cities in Jiangsu Province, one of the most competitive and leading provinces in the country in terms of education. title: Female academic leadership in private higher education: gender dynamics and leadership effectiveness
abstract: Female academic leaders remain systemically underrepresented in senior positions across higher education institutions globally, and this disparity is particularly pronounced across Asian contexts. Drawing on the authors’ collective experience as female academic leaders at IMU University a private health professions university in Malaysia and situated within the broader literature on gender and educational leadership, this Perspective examines how leadership styles, gender dynamics, institutional culture, and external influences shape the effectiveness, perception, and advancement of women in academic settings. title: Beyond passive rights-holders: toward student moral agency in assessment fairness
abstract: Over the past decade, fairness research in classroom assessment has progressively repositioned students from passive objects toward partial subjects of assessment. By advocating for student active engagement in assessment processes via discourses such as student voice and rights, student agency, student assessment literacy, and student partnership in assessment, this research has extended students’ active positioning in assessment. abstract: Purpose This study focused on Newman's error analysis (NEA) model to analyze the errors of senior high school students in solving circle theorem problems. title: Using school food gardens to promote education for sustainable development: leadership perspectives from school principals in South Africa
abstract: Introduction School food gardens are increasingly recognized as valuable contexts for advancing Education for Sustainable Development (ESD) through experiential, place-based learning. However, limited research has examined how school principals exercise leadership to support the use of school food gardens as educational spaces for sustainability learning, particularly in resource-constrained contexts. Methods This qualitative multiple-case study explored principals' leadership practices in five public primary schools in the Tshwane School District, South Africa, participating in the Transforming Education for Sustainable Futures initiative. title: Linking motivation to productivity: structural analysis of research performance in teaching–research-oriented universities in China
abstract: This study examines the relationships between research motivation and scientific research performance among faculty in teaching–research-oriented universities in China. Based on survey data from 329 faculty members, confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling were used to examine the associations between intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, avoidance motivation, and six dimensions of scientific research performance: Scientific Research Projects (RPJ), Academic Papers (PUB), Monographs (MON), Scientific Research Awards (AWA), Consultation and Decision-making Results (POL), and Technology Transfer Outputs (TRF).
